#10192. AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost

One campaign targets 105 sites using open-weight models; in another, public models gained full domain control for $12. Cyber-defense will have to change.

Over five days in September, a Chinese-speaking attacker used three different AI harnesses and both open-weight and public AI models to target 105 different e-commerce sites.

Usually within a day, and often with hours, the autonomous hacking system compromised at least 27 different companies. Malicious agents stole at least 600,000 payment card records from two, installed credit-card skimmers on the websites of five, and gained some degree of illicit access to the rest, which includes at least one Fortune 500 company, according to Gambit Security, which discovered the campaign.

The total bill for the attackers? An average of $25.46 per completed target.

"The scale and success of this campaign are remarkable for just one week, especially considering the size of some of the victims," says Sa'ar Elias, co-founder and chief research officer for Gambit Security. "Work that would previously have required a coordinated team of skilled attackers can now be carried out by one person without much prior knowledge."

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

The autonomous credit-card and data-stealing campaign is not an outlier. Agentic AI has sped up vulnerability research, leading to a massive surge in CVE assignments. Attackers are increasingly using AI to automate attacks, exploit systems faster, and even act as fully autonomous hackers.

In another instance, researchers with AI cyber-defense firm Silverfort conduct lab tests using an orchestrating agent and publicly available versions of Claude Opus to explore how quickly autonomous AI can turn initial access into a full compromise. The "attacker" gained complete domain control in eight minutes, says Colin Ferris, threat hunting and incident response lead at Silverfort.

"The barrier to entry is falling," Ferris says. "What it takes is a basic foothold, not exotic skill, and that’s why this won't stay confined to sophisticated actors."

Prices in dark markets have reflected the reduction in costs for attackers. Because of increasing supply in the underground markets, the average price of sold initial access declined from just over $1,400 to $429, according to figures from threat intelligence firm Flashpoint. While fewer companies are paying ransoms — 28% in the first half of 2026 — ransomware activity continued to grow by 45%, the company said.

"Initial access is where we've measured the price drop," says Ian Gray, vice president of intelligence for Flashpoint. "Elsewhere in the attack chain, we see AI making operations faster and easier to scale."

Related:Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit

In many ways, the situation resembles the one on current battlefields: Cheap autonomous or directed attacks by drones are making expensive defenses uneconomical, which means that defenders have to find cheaper ways to defend and harden systems. In the latest campaign, cyberattackers used the agentic AI system Hermes and two AI penetration-testing frameworks, Strix and Cairn, according to Gambit Security.

"Attackers can now launch increasingly sophisticated attacks at very low marginal costs, while defenders must maintain a high level of reliability across complex environments," says Gambit Security's Elias. "Defending against every individual attempt can quickly become an unsustainable economic proposition."

Applying AI to existing security processes will be necessary, but not enough, he says. Instead, companies need to look at their business processes, determine which ones matter most, and find ways to protect them and prevent disruption.

For the past two decades, cybersecurity experts have warned that companies can't expect to avoid attacks simply because they are in an obscure business or have a relatively small attack surface. Every part of a company that is attached to the Internet or connected to a partner connected to the Internet will be attacked, says Albert Ziegler, chief information security officer at offensive cybersecurity firm XBOW.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

"These are not incredibly expensive attacks, but also these are attacks that work because the sites haven't been hardened enough," he says. "It's that it's not enough to protect a couple of crown jewel sites that you are very concerned about."

One way to bolster defenses is to focus on the basic paths that AI agents tend to exploit — overprivileged accounts, reused credentials, and unmanaged service accounts — and automate access decisions, so humans do not slow down responses, Silverfort's Ferris says. When Silverfort researchers improved controls, especially authentication and access, the same agent that took the domain in minutes hit 21 dead ends and gave up, he says.

"AI didn't create these weaknesses; it just finds them faster," Ferris says. "Controls that stop the attack at the point of access are cheaper than cleanup afterwards."

Companies should focus on the economics of recovering from an attack and how to protect their minimum viable business processes, says Gambit Security's Elias. Business leaders should focus on what investments will have the most business impact.

Unfortunately, that may mean budgets need to grow to adapt to the economics of AI, he says. However, "spending should increasingly be measured by how effectively it protects business operations," he notes, "rather than simply how many threats or tools a security program can manage."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. #10191. NVIDIA brings agents to life with DGX Spark and Reachy Mini

Today at CES 2026, NVIDIA unveiled a world of new open models to enable the future of agents, online and in the real world. From the recently released NVIDIA Nemotron reasoning LLMs to the new NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1.6 open reasoning VLA and NVIDIA Cosmos world foundation models, all the building blocks are here today for AI Builders to build their own agents.

But what if you could bring your own agent to life, right at your desk? An AI buddy that can be useful to you and process your data privately?

In the CES keynote today, Jensen Huang showed us how we can do exactly that, using the processing power of NVIDIA DGX Spark with Reachy Mini to create your own little office R2D2 you can talk to and collaborate with.

This blog post provides a step-by-step guide to replicate this amazing experience at home using a DGX Spark and Reachy Mini.

If you want to start cooking right away, here’s the source code of the demo.

Feel free to adapt the recipe and make it your own - you have many ways to integrate the models into your application:

Turning an AI agent from a simple chat interface into something you can interact with naturally makes conversations feel more real. When an AI agent can see through a camera, speak out loud, and perform actions, the experience becomes more engaging. That’s what Reachy Mini makes possible.

Reachy Mini is designed to be customizable. With access to sensors, actuators, and APIs, you can easily wire it into your existing agent stack, by simulation or real hardware controlled directly from Python.

This post focuses on composing existing building blocks rather than reinventing them. We combine open models for reasoning and vision, an agent framework for orchestration, and tool handlers for actions. Each component is loosely coupled, making it easy to swap models, change routing logic, or add new behaviors.

Unlike closed personal assistants, this setup stays fully open. You control the models, the prompts, the tools, and the robot’s actions. Reachy Mini simply becomes the physical endpoint of your agent where perception, reasoning, and action come together.

In this example, we use the NVIDIA NeMo Agent Toolkit, a flexible, lightweight, framework-agnostic open source library, to connect all the components of the agent together. It works seamlessly with other agentic frameworks, like LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, handling how models interact, routing inputs and outputs between them, and making it easy to experiment with different configurations or add new capabilities without rewriting core logic. The toolkit also provides built-in profiling and optimization features, letting you track token usage efficiency and latency across tools and agents, identify bottlenecks, and automatically tune hyperparameters to maximize accuracy while reducing cost and latency.

First, clone the repository that contains all the code you’ll need to follow along:

To access your intelligence layer, powered by the NVIDIA Nemotron models, you can either deploy them using NVIDIA NIM or vLLM, or connect to them through remote endpoints available at build.nvidia.com.

The following instructions assume you are accessing the Nemotron models via endpoints. Create a .env file in the main directory with your API keys. For local deployments, you do not need to specify API keys and can skip this step.

Start by getting a basic LLM chat workflow running through NeMo Agent Toolkit’s API server. NeMo Agent Toolkit supports running workflows via `nat serve` and providing a config file. The config file passed here contains all the necessary setup information for the agent, which includes the models used for chat, image understanding, as well as the router model used by the agent. The NeMo Agent Toolkit UI can connect over HTTP/WebSocket so you can chat with your workflow like a standard chat product. In this implementation, the NeMo Agent Toolkit server is launched on port 8001 (so your bot can call it, and the UI can too):

Next, verify that you can send a plain text prompt through a separate terminal to ensure everything is setup correctly:

Reviewing the agent configuration, you’ll notice it defines far more capabilities than a simple chat completion. The next steps will walk through those details.

Tool calling is an essential part of AI agents. NeMo Agent Toolkit includes a built-in ReAct agent that can reason between tool calls and use multiple tools before answering. We route “action requests” to a ReAct agent that’s allowed to call tools (for example, tools that trigger robot behaviors or fetch current robot state).

Take a look at this portion of the config it defines the tools (like Wikipedia search) and specifies the ReAct agent pattern used to manage them.

The key idea: don’t use one model for everything. Instead, route based on intent:

You can implement routing a few ways (heuristics, a lightweight classifier, or a dedicated routing service). If you want the “production” version of this idea, the NVIDIA LLM Router developer example is the full reference implementation and includes evaluation and monitoring patterns.

A basic routing policy might work like this:

These sections of the config define the routing topology and specify the router model.

NOTE: If you want to reduce latency/cost or run offline, you can self-host one of the routed models (typically the “fast text” model) and keep the VLM remote. One common approach is serving via NVIDIA NIM or vLLM and pointing NeMo Agent Toolkit to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Now we go real time. Pipecat is a framework designed for low-latency voice/multimodal agents: it orchestrates audio/video streams, AI services, and transports so you can build natural conversations. In this repo, the bot service is responsible for:

You will find all the pipecat bot code in the `reachy-personal-assistant/bot` folder.

Reachy Mini exposes a daemon that the rest of your system connects to. The repo runs the daemon in simulation by default (--sim). If you have access to a real Reachy you can remove this flag and the same code will control your robot.

You will need three terminals to run the entire system:

If you are using the physical hardware, remember to omit the --sim flag from the command.

If the NeMo Agent Toolkit service is not already running from Step 1, start it now in Terminal 3.

Once all the terminals are set up, there are two main windows to keep track of:

Reachy Sim – This window appears automatically when you start the simulator daemon in Terminal 1. This is applicable if you’re running Reachy mini simulation in place of the physical device.

Pipecat Playground – This is the client-side UI where you can connect to the agent, enable microphone and camera inputs, and view live transcripts. In Terminal 2, open the URL exposed by the bot service: http://localhost:7860/. Click “CONNECT” in your browser. It may take a few seconds to initialize, and you’ll be prompted to grant microphone (and optionally camera) access.

At this point, you can start interacting with your agent!

Here are a few simple prompts to help you test your personal assistant. You can start with these and then experiment by adding your own to see how the agent responds!

Text-only prompts (routes to the fast text model)

Instead of a "black-box" assistant, this builds a foundation for a private, hackable system where you can control both the intelligence and the hardware. You can inspect, extend, and run it locally, with full visibility into data flow, tool permissions, and how the robot perceives and acts.

#10190. The Meta Quest 2 and Quest Pro are receiving their last OS updates soon. Here’s what you need to know

The best-selling VR headset of all time (and its Pro-level cousin) will no longer receive OS updates after March 2027.

Somehow, the Meta Quest 2 has been around for six whopping years, and Meta is finally bringing support for the headset to a close after March 2027. The far less popular Meta Quest Pro, which uses the same chipset as the Quest 2, will also see OS updates cease at the same time with OS v213. Meta will continue to deliver security updates through the end of 2027 to both headsets, according to an official Meta developers blog post.

Meta says it will not be removing cross-play multiplayer functionality or blocking access to Quest 2 players, so any games that support the headset will continue to work after these dates, so long as they don’t rely on any new OS features introduced after March 2027. Developers have to give players a 6-month notice if support is ending for a game, so you’ll have ample time to decide what to do.

That means the Quest 2 will receive just over 7 years of total security updates, while the Quest Pro gets two years less (since it came out in October 2022). The Meta Quest 2 remains the best-selling VR headset of all time, with around 20 million units sold over the lifetime of the headset. Meta says that Quest 2 owners can still play games throughout this time, although game support will likely dry up quickly after January 2028.

The $599 Meta Quest 3 and $349 Meta Quest 3S, which debuted in 2023 and 2024, respectively, are the follow-ups to the Quest 2. This move could help data centers operate sooner without waiting for the rest of the grid to catch up to its peak demand.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Electricity consumption is one of the biggest concerns that residents bring up whenever a data center is proposed in their community, which is why OpenAI is taking steps to minimize its impact on the local electricity grid. According to the company, its Grid Protectors Program aims to reduce the power consumption of its data centers as local demand increases, ensuring that the grid is not overwhelmed during peak hours. Aside from ensuring that the lights remain on for everyone, it would also allow its data centers to connect to the grid and go online sooner instead of waiting for the additional power sources to come online.

“Whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity. Our goal is to make campus flexibility a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most,” OpenAI said in its blog. It also added, “Through Grid Protectors, our ambition is to make this kind of flexibility a core part of how we build and operate future campuses. That means designing facilities to reduce electricity use when needed and working with utilities to agree on how much demand can be reduced, how quickly and for how long. The arrangements will differ by location, and we will share additional commitments as they are finalized.”

OpenAI is testing the program in its planned Effingham County campus in Georgia, with the company saying that it has already signed a 3.2-gigawatt agreement with Georgia Power that included 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response. This ensures that if demand jumps on the hottest days of the year, there would be enough power to accommodate the hundreds of thousands of air conditioners keeping Georgians cool. With the average American home drawing around 1,200 kilowatts, the 1,000-megawatt buffer is more than enough to power around 800,000 households — nearly 20% of the state’s homes.

This technology, called demand response, has been around for decades now, where large operators reduce their demand in response to a peak in demand from other consumers. Before automation, grid operators would manually call up industrial customers like steel mills and ask them to cut consumption to ensure the reliability of the entire grid. But with modern technologies and IoT, it can now be done automatically, allowing data centers to reduce their load in under a minute. In fact, Nvidia has already been experimenting with a similar system in the UK and has proven that it works.

#10187. Introducing Falcon-H1-Arabic: Pushing the Boundaries of Arabic Language AI with Hybrid Architecture

Discover more in our official blogpost, featuring an interactive experience

The journey of building world-class Arabic language models has been one of continuous learning and iteration. Today, we're excited to announce Falcon-H1-Arabic, our most advanced Arabic language model family to date, representing a significant leap forward in both architecture and capabilities. This release embodies months of research, community feedback, and technical innovation, culminating in three powerful models that set new standards for Arabic natural language processing.

When we launched Falcon-Arabic a few months ago, the response from the community was both humbling and enlightening. Developers, researchers and students across the Arab world used the model for real use cases, pushing them to its limits and providing invaluable feedback. We learned where the model excelled and, more importantly, where it struggled. Long-context understanding, dialectal variations, mathematical reasoning, and domain-specific knowledge emerged as key areas requiring deeper attention.

We didn't just want to make incremental improvements, we wanted to fundamentally rethink our approach. The result is Falcon-H1-Arabic, a model family that addresses every piece of feedback we received while introducing architectural innovations that were previously unexplored in Arabic language modeling.

Falcon-H1-Arabic 3B, 7B, 34B models outperforming all SOTA models of similar sizes and sometimes bigger.

Falcon-H1-Arabic is built on the Falcon-H1 hybrid architecture, which integrates State Space Models (Mamba) and Transformer attention within every block. Both components run in parallel and their representations are fused before the block’s output projection. This design provides the linear-time scalability of Mamba for extremely long sequences while preserving the precise long-range modeling capabilities of attention. For Arabic, with its rich morphology and flexible sentence structures, this approach significantly improves coherence and reasoning across extended text. We've deployed this architecture across three scales (3B, 7B, 34B parameters), each balancing capacity, efficiency, and deployability for different use cases from edge devices to enterprise applications.

Falcon-H1 architecture. Attention and SSM run in parallel within each block; their outputs are concatenated before the block’s output projection. The number of SSM/Attention heads depends on the model size. More details on the Falcon-H1 technical report.

We've dramatically increased context capabilities from Falcon-Arabic's 32K limit to 128K tokens for the 3B model and 256K tokens for both the 7B and 34B models. At 256K tokens (~200,000 words), these models can process several novels or hundreds of pages of technical documentation enabling applications in legal analysis, medical records, academic research, and extended conversations that were previously impractical. Our post-training specifically addresses "lost in the middle" challenges to ensure models effectively utilize their full context range, not just accept long inputs.

We rebuilt our pre-training data pipeline from the ground up to better reflect the complexity of Arabic. This began with a multi-stage quality filtering process tailored to Arabic orthography, morphology, diacritics, and syntactic patterns. Instead of heuristic filtering, we used deep linguistic analysis to isolate coherent, well-structured text and remove noise commonly found in open-web corpora. The result is a significantly cleaner, more stylistically consistent Arabic dataset.

Dialect coverage was another key priority. Arabic is not monolithic; Modern Standard Arabic coexists with dialects such as Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, and Maghrebi, each with distinct vocabularies and grammatical constructions. We expanded dialectal sources substantially so the models would understand and generate the full spectrum of real-world Arabic rather than leaning disproportionately toward formal MSA. To maintain global reasoning and domain diversity, we also preserved the multilingual capabilities of Falcon-H1 by training the Arabic models on an almost equal mix of Arabic, English, and multilingual content totalling around 300 Billion Tokens. This ensures strong performance in code, STEM, and cross-lingual reasoning. The following figure illustrates the distribution of the pre-training data across languages and categories. All values are expressed in billions of tokens.

After pre-training, Falcon-H1-Arabic undergoes a focused post-training pipeline consisting of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). During SFT, we expose the models to high-quality Arabic instructions, curated long-context examples, and structured reasoning tasks that teach them to follow directives, maintain coherence over extended sequences, and ground their responses in relevant information. This stage is crucial for ensuring that the models can actually use their large context windows which does not emerge automatically from architecture alone.

We follow SFT with a targeted DPO phase to refine alignment, conversational quality, and preference consistency. DPO helps the models balance long-context reasoning with general linguistic competence, improving helpfulness and reducing common failure modes such as drifting, overuse of context, or neglecting earlier information. Throughout both stages, we carefully monitor for catastrophic forgetting and maintain a controlled curriculum so gains in long-context behavior do not come at the expense of core reasoning or factual accuracy. The result is a family of models that handles extended documents and dialogue with ease while preserving strong performance on everyday language tasks.

Beyond benchmark-oriented optimization, our post-training process deliberately strengthens areas that traditional evaluations do not fully capture, including conversational faithfulness, rhetorical organization, structured follow-ups, and discourse coherence. These enhancements significantly boost the model’s practical usefulness, making Falcon-H1-Arabic more dependable in real multi-turn dialogue, instruction execution, and long-context conversational flows.

Numbers tell an important part of the story. On the Open Arabic LLM Leaderboard (OALL), a comprehensive benchmark evaluating Arabic language understanding across diverse tasks, Falcon-H1-Arabic achieves state-of-the-art results at every scale we tested. Note that our scores may vary slightly from those reported on the leaderboard, as we used vLLM as the backend instead of the leaderboard’s Accelerate-based implementation. These differences are typically under one point while offering significantly faster runtime.

Beyond OALL, we also report results on the 3LM benchmark for STEM-related tasks on both synthetic and native splits; Arabculture for Arabic culture assessment; and AraDice for Arabic dialect coverage across Levantine, and Egyptian varieties as well as Arabic culture across 6 countries. The reported AraDice score is the average of all the 3 scores.

Starting with the 3B model, the performance is exceptional. It reaches approximately 62% on OALL, outperforming all small-scale models, including Gemma-4B, Qwen3-4B, and Phi-4-mini by roughly ten points. On 3LM, the main Arabic STEM benchmark, it scores around 82% on the native split and 73% on the synthetic split. It also achieves about 62% on the ArabCulture benchmark and around 50% across AraDice dialect evaluation (Egyptian, Gulf, and Levantine). This makes Falcon-H1-Arabic-3B a high-quality, highly efficient model suitable for edge deployments, real-time applications, and agentic systems where latency and cost matter.

The 7B model continues this upward trajectory. With a score of 71.7% on OALL, it surpasses all models in the ~10B class, including Fanar-9B, Allam-7B*, and Qwen3-8B. On 3LM, it reaches about 92% on the native split and 85% on the synthetic one. AraDice scores rise into the mid-50s across all dialects, and ArabCulture results approach 80%. This model strikes an ideal balance between capability and deployability, making it the most practical choice for general-purpose Arabic NLP in production environments.

The 34B model represents our flagship system and establishes a new state of the art for Arabic language modeling. It reaches approximately 75% on OALL, outperforming not only models of similar size but even much larger systems such as Llama-3.3-70B and AceGPT2-32B. Its 3LM scores reach about 96% on the native split and 94% on the synthetic one. On ArabCulture it scores close to 80%, and on AraDice it reaches around 53 across dialects. The fact that a 34B hybrid model surpasses the performance of 70B-scale transformers demonstrates the effectiveness of the Falcon-H1 architecture, the quality of the data, and the strength of the post-training pipeline.

These benchmark results validate our approach but also highlight an important reality: the frontier of Arabic language modeling is advancing rapidly. Each percentage point on these benchmarks represents countless hours of engineering effort, careful dataset curation, and architectural refinement. The margins by which Falcon-H1-Arabic leads aren't just statistical artifacts, they translate to meaningfully better user experiences in real-world applications.

Each model in the Falcon-H1-Arabic family is suited to different deployment scenarios. The 3B model is optimized for speed, cost-efficiency, and high-throughput systems, making it ideal for agentic workflows, on-device applications, low-latency chat, and environments with strict resource constraints. The 7B model serves as the general-purpose workhorse for most production applications, powering document understanding systems, chatbots, summarization pipelines, and content generation tools. The 34B model is designed for high-stakes domains where accuracy and long-range reasoning matter most, including legal analysis, medical summarization, academic research, and large-scale enterprise automation. Its extended context window makes it uniquely capable of analyzing hundreds of pages of text in a single pass while maintaining precise coherence.

Like all language models, Falcon-H1-Arabic may reflect biases from training data and can produce hallucinated information. Model outputs should not be used as sole authorities for medical, legal, or financial decisions without professional verification. Long-context performance may degrade at extreme ranges. We recommend task-specific evaluation and appropriate guardrails before deployment in production or sensitive applications.

This work stands on the shoulders of many. We extend our gratitude to the Arabic NLP research community, whose open sharing of benchmarks, datasets, and methodologies enables progress across the field. Special thanks to our colleagues at TII: Ilyas Chahed, Younes Belkada, Dhia Eddine Rhaiem, Puneesh Khanna, Jingwei Zuo, Mikhail Lubinets, Slim Frikha, Maksim Velikanov, Kacper Piskorski, and Suhail Mohmad for their invaluable support during this project.

Track, rank and evaluate open Arabic LLMs and chatbots

Impressive milestone for Arabic language AI. Falcon-H1-Arabic’s hybrid architecture is a strong step toward closing the performance gap in high-quality Arabic understanding and generation. Exciting to see innovation that’s not just scaling models, but rethinking architecture to better capture the richness and complexity of Arabic. #10186. Building CRM Automations That Don't Break: APIs, Webhooks, and AI Validation

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Modern businesses rarely struggle with a shortage of software. The bigger problem is getting their existing systems to communicate properly.

A lead arrives through a website form, but the sales team doesn't receive a notification. Someone books an appointment, yet their CRM record isn't updated. A prospect replies to an automated message, but the follow-up sequence continues as though nothing happened.

These are integration problems rather than software problems.

Platforms such as GoHighLevel aim to solve them by combining contact management, messaging, appointment scheduling and workflow automation in one environment. However, the real value comes from how these components are configured and connected to other applications.

For developers, agencies and technical consultants, GoHighLevel provides an interesting example of how low-code automation and API-driven development can work together.

This guide explores the architecture behind an effective CRM automation system, how GoHighLevel's integrations operate, and where custom development makes sense. The patterns below — data normalisation, idempotent event handling, queue-based processing and validated AI outputs — apply to any CRM; GoHighLevel is used here as the running example because it combines native workflows with a public API and webhooks in one platform.

It's tempting to think of automation as a collection of simple rules.

When someone submits a form, send an email. When a customer books a meeting, update their status. When a payment arrives, trigger a notification.

Individually, these are straightforward tasks.

Problems emerge when different workflows start interacting.

Consider a business that generates leads through several channels:

Referral partners and external lead providers

Each channel introduces different information, sometimes in different formats.

One source might supply a full name, phone number and email address. Another provides only a phone number. A third might include campaign information, product preferences or qualification answers.

Without a consistent data structure, CRM records become fragmented. Duplicate contacts appear, important information disappears and automations begin acting on incomplete data.

A well-designed system needs to address these problems before adding more workflow complexity.

GoHighLevel combines native workflow tools with an API that allows developers to integrate external services.

Its core components include contact records, conversations, calendars, opportunities, pipelines and workflow automation.

Developers can interact with supported resources through the platform's REST API, while webhooks provide a mechanism for reacting to events.

Information enters the system through forms, funnels, integrations, inbound communication or API requests.

At this stage, the priority is collecting reliable information and associating it with the correct contact.

Once information has been received, workflows can evaluate conditions and initiate actions.

For example, a newly created lead might trigger an internal notification, a qualification sequence or an appointment invitation.

Some business processes require functionality beyond the CRM's native capabilities.

An organisation might need to synchronise an accounting platform, update an external database or pass information into a proprietary application.

This is where APIs, webhooks and middleware become especially useful.

The important architectural decision is determining which tasks belong inside the CRM and which should be handled externally.

GoHighLevel's developer platform offers REST endpoints for supported operations involving contacts, conversations, calendars, payments and other CRM resources.

Its API uses JSON and supports token-based authentication, including OAuth 2.0 for applications requiring delegated access.

For developers creating an internal integration, a Private Integration Token may be appropriate. Public applications serving multiple accounts generally require a different authentication architecture.

A basic API request follows a familiar pattern:

This example illustrates the structure of a contact-creation request. Production implementations should validate the current endpoint schema, manage tokens securely, handle retries and consider using an upsert operation when duplicate prevention is required.

Two production details deserve attention up front. First, treat a 429 rate-limit response as a normal control signal, not an error: back off exponentially, respect any retry-after value, and never retry in a tight loop. Second, prefer upserts keyed on a stable identifier (a normalised phone number or email address) over blind creates, so a retried request cannot spawn a duplicate contact.

The same principles apply when synchronising information from external applications.

For example, an insurance business might receive enquiries through a specialist quoting system. Rather than manually transferring those records, an integration could normalise the information and send it to the CRM.

The key is to treat the API as part of a broader data architecture, not merely as another way to trigger messages.

APIs are useful when an application needs to retrieve or modify information.

Webhooks address a different requirement: knowing when something has happened.

A webhook-driven architecture might look like this:

A configured webhook sends event data to an external endpoint.

The receiving application verifies and processes the event.

This is particularly useful when connecting CRM activity to internal dashboards, fulfilment systems or custom databases.

However, webhook integrations require careful handling.

A publicly accessible webhook endpoint shouldn't automatically trust every request it receives.

Where the platform provides signature verification, developers should validate the signature using the documented method before processing the payload. In practice this means computing an HMAC over the raw request body with the shared signing secret and comparing it to the signature header in constant time — never parsing the body first and re-serialising it, which can change the bytes the signature was computed over.

If an appointment event triggers an invoice, processing the same event twice could create duplicate invoices.

An idempotent handler should recognise an event that has already been processed and avoid repeating side effects. The reliable way to do this is to store each event's unique ID (or a hash of its payload) in a small processed-events table and check it before running any side effect — a duplicate delivery then becomes a cheap no-op instead of a second invoice.

Long-running operations shouldn't necessarily execute inside the initial webhook request.

A more resilient approach is to validate the event, record it, acknowledge receipt and place any substantial work on a processing queue. Return a 2xx response within a second or two so the sender does not retry, then let a worker handle the slow steps. Failed jobs should retry with exponential backoff and, after a set number of attempts, land in a dead-letter queue where a human can inspect them instead of being retried forever.

This helps prevent slow third-party services from disrupting event handling.

Consider a company receiving enquiries through paid advertising, website forms and telephone calls.

The objective is simple: respond quickly, qualify potential customers and book appointments.

A practical CRM workflow could follow several stages.

Incoming data should be converted into a consistent format.

Phone numbers should be standardised, source information should be preserved, and duplicate detection should be considered before creating another contact.

It's also important to retain communication preferences and the relevant consent information.

Not every lead should be distributed randomly.

Assignment logic might consider geographical territory, product category, team availability or an existing customer relationship.

For more complicated organisations, routing decisions may need to be calculated in an external service.

Once the lead has been assigned, the system can initiate an appropriate follow-up.

This might involve notifying a sales representative, sending a permitted acknowledgement or offering an appointment booking link.

The workflow needs to respond to changing circumstances.

If the prospect books an appointment, unnecessary booking reminders should stop.

If a sales representative takes ownership, automated outreach may need to pause.

If the prospect opts out, the system must respect that preference across relevant communication channels.

Finally, the system should record what happened.

Useful measurements include lead response time, appointment booking rate, appointment attendance and conversion rate.

These metrics make it possible to distinguish a workflow that simply runs from one that improves business operations.

Artificial intelligence introduces additional possibilities, particularly around lead qualification, conversation handling and information extraction.

An AI-powered system might analyse an incoming enquiry, identify the customer's requirements and suggest an appropriate next action.

It could also summarise a conversation for a sales representative or help classify enquiries into different service categories.

However, introducing an AI model creates new engineering considerations.

Allowing an AI model to generate unrestricted text is rarely sufficient when that output controls business processes.

A more predictable approach is to require structured responses and validate them before updating CRM records.

The application should check that the response matches the expected schema before performing any action.

Some actions are better handled by deterministic rules.

Communication consent, payment processing, account permissions and important customer record changes shouldn't depend solely on a language model's interpretation.

AI can help classify or summarise information, but critical operations should remain subject to validated rules and appropriate human oversight.

AI assistants can reduce repetitive work, but they should also recognise their limitations.

A prospect asking an unusual technical question or requesting a customised proposal may need to speak with a person.

The best automation systems provide clear escalation paths rather than trying to automate every possible interaction.

GoHighLevel's visual workflow builder makes many routine automations accessible to non-developers.

A basic appointment reminder or lead notification may require little custom development.

The situation changes when several systems need to work together.

For example, a business might need to migrate thousands of existing contacts, integrate custom booking software, synchronise records with an accounting platform and implement specialised lead routing.

These projects require more than familiarity with a visual workflow editor.

They involve data modelling, integration architecture, testing, security and operational reliability.

The decision rule is straightforward: use native workflows for anything the platform already does well, and write custom code only where the platform's model runs out — multi-source routing, external system synchronisation, or reporting that spans several platforms. That distinction matters because unnecessary custom development can make a system harder to maintain, while forcing every process into native workflows can create an equally fragile architecture.

Even technically capable teams can run into problems when implementing CRM integrations.

Large workflows containing dozens of branches are difficult to test and maintain.

Smaller, clearly defined workflows are generally easier to troubleshoot.

An integration that works with ten contacts may behave very differently when processing thousands of records.

Developers should account for rate limits, batch processing, exponential backoff and retry behaviour.

Creating a new contact for every incoming event can quickly damage CRM data quality.

Contact matching, normalisation and carefully selected identifiers help reduce duplication.

Access tokens should never be exposed in client-side JavaScript or committed to public repositories.

Use appropriate secret management and grant integrations only the permissions they require.

Successful execution doesn't necessarily mean the system behaves correctly.

Test scenarios should cover missing information, duplicate events, failed API requests, appointment cancellations, opt-outs and unexpected responses from external services.

Observability matters too. Logs and alerts should help identify which step failed and whether the operation can be retried safely.

Not every automation problem needs an API integration.

A useful decision framework is to start with the simplest reliable implementation.

Standard appointment reminders — Native CRM workflows

Basic lead assignment — Native workflows where supported

External application synchronisation — API or integration middleware

Complex routing across several data sources — Custom logic with CRM integration

AI-assisted lead classification — AI service with validated outputs

Enterprise reporting across multiple platforms — Dedicated reporting or data pipeline

Hybrid architectures are often the most practical.

The CRM manages customer interactions and standard business processes, while specialised services handle requirements that benefit from custom code.

This separation can also make future maintenance more manageable.

CRM automation has become considerably more accessible, but ease of implementation shouldn't be confused with reliability.

A workflow that sends a message after a form submission is easy to demonstrate. A system that handles thousands of contacts, prevents duplication, respects communication preferences, synchronises multiple applications and recovers gracefully from failures requires more careful design.

GoHighLevel provides a useful foundation for combining customer management with automation, particularly when its native capabilities are supported by well-designed integrations.

For developers, the opportunity isn't simply to automate more tasks. It's to design systems that remain understandable, maintainable and reliable as businesses grow.

The strongest implementations aren't necessarily the ones with the most workflows, API connections or AI features.

They're the ones where the right information reaches the right system at the right time — and everything continues working when something inevitably goes wrong.

Microsoft's claimed performance gains will need to be tested

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Following a resurgence of 8GB RAM laptops earlier this year, and in the wake of promises to improve Windows 11 performance using just 8GB of RAM, Microsoft has today announced what it claims are a series of performance improvements. Driven by an ongoing global PC component shortage that is forcing manufacturers to dumb down specs, the company says that with 8GB of RAM, Windows is now 20% more responsive and 40% faster when it comes to multitasking.

The development shared today by Microsoft is an update to a commitment earlier this year to improve the quality and performance of Windows 11, a major bugbear of users since its launch. Microsoft says it has taken a three-pronged approach to memory optimization: making better use of memory in Windows 11 PCs, protecting interactions that need to feel instant, and ensuring key apps and Windows use less memory. While the company admits you'll be able to do more on 16GB or 32GB of RAM, it says "we're making sure you can do more, even with 8GB."

The headline performance gain is a claim that Windows is now up to 20% more responsive on 8GB PCs. Likewise, multitasking is now purportedly 40% faster in Microsoft's lab tests. Of course, these are internal tests conducted in favorable conditions by Microsoft.

Microsoft says it has tuned compression for useful apps and data, and can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory, rather than moving it to storage. In practice, this should mean that apps and tabs left open should be less likely to reload when you go back to them.

The claim of 20% more responsiveness specifically relates to tasks like opening Start, searching, right-clicking, opening Settings, using the Snipping Tool, and opening File Explorer. The company says it has achieved this by backing off background tasks like indexing while you're using your PC actively. Edge now reportedly opens up to 33% faster. There's also an Efficiency Mode for Microsoft Teams, which can be set to on by default, improving launch times by 20%.

Microsoft says that its claims of 40% speed boosts to multitasking are based on a demanding workflow of 20 Microsoft Edge Tabs, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, Outlook, and File Explorer all being opened one after the other.

Other improvements include reducing committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB in apps like Microsoft Edge and 365 apps, and reducing the memory footprint of Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook by 360MB. Third-party apps can also benefit from improved memory management, with Microsoft stating WhatsApp is already taking advantage.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Moving forward, Microsoft says it has plans to make memory compression even smarter and more efficient. Windows features and apps will share common parts, such as Search and Widgets using one web Engine, for instance. WinUI 3 apps like File Explorer and Notepad will be designed to use less memory and open faster, and Microsoft is working with PC makers and silicon manufacturers to reduce how much memory a PC needs to hold in reserve to support its hardware, making more space for Windows.

#10183. NVIDIA Cosmos Reason 2 Brings Advanced Reasoning To Physical AI

NVIDIA today released Cosmos Reason 2, the latest advancement in open, reasoning vision language models for physical AI. Cosmos Reason 2 surpasses its previous version in accuracy and tops the Physical AI Bench and Physical Reasoning leaderboards as the #1 open model for visual understanding.

Since their introduction, vision-language models have rapidly improved at tasks like object and pattern recognition in images. But they still struggle with tasks humans find natural, like planning several steps ahead, dealing with uncertainty or adapting to new situations. Cosmos Reason is designed to close this gap by giving robots and AI agents stronger common sense and reasoning to solve complex problems step by step.

Cosmos Reason 2 is a state-of-the-art, open reasoning vision-language model (VLM) that enables robots and AI agents to see, understand, plan, and act in the physical world like humans. It uses common sense, physics, and prior knowledge to recognize how objects move across space and time to handle complex tasks, adapt to new situations, and figure out how to solve problems step by step.

Improved spatio-temporal understanding and timestamp precision.

Optimized performance with flexible deployment options from edge to cloud with 2B and 8B parameters model sizes.

Support for expanded set of spatial understanding and visual perception capabilities — 2D/3D point localization, bounding box coordinates, trajectory data, and OCR support.

Improved long-context understanding with 256K input tokens, up from 16K with Cosmos Reason 1.

Adaptable to multiple use cases with easy-to-use Cosmos Cookbook recipes.

Video analytics AI agents — These agents can extract valuable insights from massive volumes of video data to optimize processes. Cosmos Reason 2 builds on the capabilities of Cosmos Reason 1 and now provides OCR support, as well as 2D/3D point localization and a set of mark understanding.

Developers can jumpstart development of video analytics AI agents by using the NVIDIA blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) with Cosmos Reason as the VLM.

Salesforce is transforming workplace safety and compliance by analyzing video footage captured by Cobalt robots with Agentforce and VSS blueprint with Cosmos Reason as the VLM.

Data annotation and critique — Enable developers to automate high-quality annotation and critique of massive, diverse training datasets. Cosmos Reason provides time stamps and detailed descriptions for real or synthetically generated training videos.

Uber is exploring Cosmos Reason 2 to deliver accurate, searchable video captions for autonomous vehicle (AV) training data, enabling efficient identification of critical driving scenarios. This co-authored Reason 2 for AV Video Captioning and VQA recipe demonstrates how to fine-tune and evaluate Cosmos Reason 2-8B on annotated AV videos. Across multiple evaluation metrics, measurable improvements were achieved: BLEU scores improved 10.6% (0.113 → 0.125), MCQ-based VQA gained 0.67 percentage points (80.18% → 80.85%), and LingoQA increased 13.8% (63.2% → 77.0%). These gains demonstrate effective domain adaptation for AV applications.

Robot planning and reasoning — Act as the brain for deliberate, methodical decision-making in a robot vision language action (VLA) model. Cosmos Reason 2 now provides trajectory coordinates in addition to determining next steps.

Encord provides native support for Cosmos Reason 2 in its Data Agent library and AI data platform, enabling developers to leverage Cosmos Reason 2 as a VLA for robotics and other physical AI use cases.

Companies like Hitachi, Milestone and VAST Data are using Cosmos Reason to advance robotics, autonomous driving, and video analytics AI agents for traffic and workplace safety.

Try Cosmos Reason 2 on build.nvidia.com and experience the latest features with sample prompts for generating bounding boxes and robot trajectories. Upload your own videos and images for further analysis.

Download Cosmos Reason 2 models (2B and 8B) on Hugging Face or use Cosmos Reason 2 in the cloud. The model will be available soon on Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. To get started, check out Cosmos Reason 2 documentation and the Cosmos Cookbook.

Cosmos Predict is a generative AI model that predicts future states of the physical world as video, based on text, image, or video inputs.

Cosmos Transfer is our lightest multicontrol model built for video to world style transfer.

NVIDIA GR00T N1.6 is an open reasoning vision language action (VLA) model, purpose-built for humanoid robots, that unlocks full body control and uses NVIDIA Cosmos Reason for better reasoning and contextual understanding.

#10182. Android gaming is having a renaissance

Good morning! Today I’m mourning the loss of Patrick Stewart by rewatching First Contact, my favorite Trek movie; beginning a marathon listen of at least one great Star Trek podcast; and replaying Elite Force and Armada, both wonderful Trek games released in 2000.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

I’m starting this edition of Inbox a bit later than I’d like, but for a good reason: I got swept up by the subject I was researching. See, I wanted to write about the seeming renaissance of gaming on Android, which has always had clear advantages and disadvantages compared to iOS. On the plus side, its openness bred experimentation and a healthy indie gaming scene, along with a thriving emulation ecosystem born of its ability to sideload apps and gain access to Android’s underlying file system. On the downside, its device and OS version fragmentation has kept some developers from attempting challenging console and PC ports, and led others to abandon their titles to bugs and time.

But thanks to a confluence of factors, as well as form factors, Android gaming is in a very good place right now. Despite Google’s continued ambivalence towards paid and premium games, the platform has received official ports of console hits like Dredge and Sifu, with others like Replaced, Absolum, and Dispatch coming soon. (One could argue things have been good for a while with Stardew Valley, Dead Cells, Balatro, Slay the Spire, and Vampire Crawlers available already, but I digress.)

Most of these games are embracing a try-before-you-buy model to avoid the upfront cost that so many mobile users resist, while others, like Dispatch, are getting a mobile optimization that reorients the experience for a portrait display.

And while traditional emulation has existed since Android was young, recent months have seen considerable improvement in breadth and performance, aided by AI coding tools and a community that wants to play its library of Steam, Windows, and Switch games on phones. This rabbit hole is extensive and varied: WinNative combines work from Winlator Bionic and Pluvia to run Windows games on Android and connect PC storefront libraries. DroidDeck aims for a SteamOS-like experience, putting Steam’s Big Picture interface on supported Android hardware with Windows games running through ARM64 Proton, which debuted recently with the Steam Frame.

It’s via DroidDeck that I whiled away a couple of glorious hours on my Galaxy Z Fold 8 playing Lumines Arise, a game perfectly suited to the pick-up-and-play nature of smartphones (though it’s best with a controller). The latest Qualcomm chips have long outpaced the mobile games they’ve been asked to power, but few knew just how well they’d run demanding PC and console titles, even through compatibility layers like Proton.

Similarly, an Android branch of the increasingly popular nxnative, which compiles Switch and Switch 2 games for iOS and macOS, has been making it easy to play games like Super Mario Bros. Wonder and Metroid Dread at 60fps on many recent Qualcomm-powered devices. There’s even a Switch 2 version in the works for Android.

The big question is whether all of this works well: will people spend more time arguing with the software than playing the games themselves? And on the legal side of the business, will publishers find success selling discounted versions of AAA titles on Android now that the translation tools are better and the device compatibility much broader?

If there’s one thing I’ve learned covering Android for nearly 20 years, it’s that the community always finds a way.

ICYMI: Ben’s Weekender essay is all about how Motorola is filling the gap OnePlus left behind, mostly.

The strangest thing I’ve seen recently is the rumor that Elon Musk wants to launch a Starlink-branded terrestrial wireless carrier in the US. Now we know how he plans to do it: by purchasing Boost Mobile from EchoStar and leveraging its contracts with AT&T and T-Mobile along with new low- and mid-band spectrum Starlink recently acquired. That infrastructure, combined with Starlink’s existing array of LEO satellites, could make for a compelling advantage over the incumbents: namely, that dead spots practically won’t exist anymore.

But as we’ve learned from countless examples over the years, running a low-margin, high-churn postpaid wireless business is not for the faint of heart, and I’m not sure why Musk has decided that now is the right time to do it.

Five years on, is the Pixel 6 series really the disaster that we remember it being? The answer, according to Damien Wilde, is a bit more nuanced.

The Pixel 6 and Pixel 6 Pro were fundamentally flawed pioneers for Google. They were the firm’s most ambitious hardware undertaking to date, and simultaneously one of the most frustrating phone series to live with during their initial launch window and beyond. If the Pixel 5 was a safe play ahead of this big pitch, the Pixel 6 was a risky dive into deep waters. It stumbled badly. Yet without those painful growing pains, the more polished, confident, and reliable Pixel devices we enjoy today simply would not exist.

Finally, networked supermarket freezers in Sweden, Belgium, and Luxembourg were hacked over the weekend, sending temperatures up to a reported 50 degrees Celsius, and all the food inside them straight into the trash.

According to Reuters, “The latest incidents follow an attack in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers at U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Army Research Laboratory (ARL) recently successfully flew the VICTOR hybrid electric drone with a heavy-fuel rotary engine, rapidly developed thanks to metal 3D printing — allowing the drone to extract more performance out of the denser but less volatile military fuel source.

The heavy fuel (JP8) used in the drone is a denser kerosene-based fuel source compared to regular jet fuel, making it desirable to reduce total fuel load or increase mileage. The JP8 fuel is part of the military’s initiative to power as much of its gas equipment on a single fuel source. However, JP8 is less volatile and harder to atomize, making it a challenge to achieve peak efficiency. Furthermore, the fuel’s flash point is 140℉, compared to gasoline’s -40℉, requiring the engine to have a much higher compression to ignite it, making pressure leaks a common issue.

JP-8 fuel on aircraft and drones is not uncommon; however, the ARL researchers wanted to further optimize the heavy-fuel rotary engine to extract more performance and improve its design. The researchers used computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and a clean-sheet design (designing from scratch, essentially), allowing the engineers to come up with more innovative solutions to get more out of the engine with less.

"The use of advanced manufacturing, including 3D metal printing, allowed us to rapidly redesign engine components based on lessons learned through experimentation,” Dr. Kweon, one of the ARL researchers, said to Army.mil. Dr. Kweon further explained that 3D printing allowed them to design an air-cooled engine and ditch a bulky liquid cooling system, reducing the size of the propulsion system. The rapid iteration eventually allowed the researchers to improve fuel atomization and decrease compression leaks.

The heavy-fuel rotary engine doesn’t actually drive the drone’s propellers directly; it uses the engine to spin a 400-volt motor-generator to generate electricity to drive the propeller motors, allowing the engine to spin independently at its most optimal RPM — similar to some hybrid EVs on the road today, except that the engine doesn’t have a mechanical link to the propellers. This system may include a battery for the drone to fly without the engine running; however, the US military has not disclosed much about the VICTOR drone’s battery configuration.

The VICTOR drone is a vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) unmanned aircraft, able to fly without a runway. The US Army has shared a video of its first flight, and the drone is able to land and take off in terrain that would otherwise be impossible for other non-VTOL two-winged aircraft. With a battery system, the drone could cover large distances on a single fuel-up, and air-cooling gives it another layer of robustness, avoiding maintenance on a liquid cooling system.

#10180. Google’s Ocarina of Time easter egg is a blast from the past

If you’re sick of AI search and all the business of modern Google search, this week’s Google easter egg will take you back 28 years to a simpler time when Ocarina of Time was the pinnacle of gaming, and Google was still a new name.

It’s hard to believe I was sitting on a couch in my parents’ living room 28 years ago, playing Ocarina of Time on my Nintendo 64. Apparently, the folks at Google feel just as nostalgic as I do about the upcoming release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo Switch 2.

Case in point, if you go to Google right now and search for “Zelda” or “Ocarina of Time,” you’ll see a Master Sword appear in the bottom-right corner of your screen. Even the “I’m Feeling Lucky” button works!

Unfortunately, the theme only works for this specific search, so you can’t keep things looking retro if you search for anything else, even if you start from the old-school search box on the 1998-themed page. Bummer. Tapping the Master Sword again brings you back to 2026 Google search, complete with a great little animation and sounds of Link in adult or child form, depending on which way you travel in time. Try it for yourself on desktop or mobile!

#10179. Open Responses: What you need to know

Open Responses is a new and open inference standard. Initiated by OpenAI, built by the open source AI community, and backed by the Hugging Face ecosystem, Open Responses is based on the Responses API and is designed for the future of Agents. In this blog post, we’ll look at how Open Responses works and why the open source community should use Open Responses.

The era of the chatbot is long gone, and agents dominate inference workloads. Developers are shifting toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act over long-time horizons. Despite this shift, much of the ecosystem still uses the Chat Completion format, which was designed for turn-based conversations and falls short for agentic use cases. The Responses format was designed to address these limitations, but it is closed and not as widely adopted. The Chat Completion format is still the de facto standard despite the alternatives.

This mismatch between the agentic workflow requirements and entrenched interfaces motivates the need for an open inference standard. Over the coming months, we will collaborate with the community and inference providers to implement and adapt Open Responses to a shared format, practically capable of replacing chat completions.

Open Responses builds on the direction OpenAI has set with their Responses API launched in March 2025, which superseded the existing Completion and Assistants APIs with a consistent way to:

Open Responses extends and open-sources the Responses API, making it more accessible for builders and routing providers to interoperate and collaborate on shared interests.

We’ll briefly explore the core changes that impact most community members. If you want to deep dive into the specification, check out the Open Responses documentation.

Client requests to Open Responses are similar to the existing Responses API. Below we demonstrate a request to the Open Responses API using curl. We're calling a proxy endpoint that routes to Inference Providers using the Open Responses API schema.

Clients that already support the Responses API can migrate to Open Responses with relatively little effort. The main changes involve how reasoning content is exposed:

OpenAI models used to only expose summary and encrypted_content. With Open Responses, providers may expose their raw reasoning via the API. Clients migrating from providers that previously returned only summaries and encrypted content will now have the opportunity to receive and handle raw reasoning streams when supported by their chosen provider.

For Model Providers, implementing the changes for Open Responses should be straightforward if they already adhere to the Responses API specification. For Routers, there is now the opportunity to standardize on a consistent endpoint and support configuration options for customization where needed.

Over time, as Providers continue to innovate, certain features will become standardized in the base specification.

In summary, migrating to Open Responses will make the inference experience more consistent and improve quality as undocumented extensions, interpretations, and workarounds of the legacy Completions API are normalized in Open Responses.

You can see how to stream reasoning chunks below.

Here’s the difference between getting an Open Response and using OpenAI Responses for reasoning deltas:

Open Responses distinguishes between “Model Providers” — those who provide inference — and “Routers” — intermediaries who orchestrate between multiple providers.

Clients can now specify a Provider along with provider-specific API options when making requests, allowing intermediary Routers to orchestrate requests between upstream providers.

Open Responses natively supports two categories of tools: internal and external. Externally hosted tools are implemented outside the model provider’s system. For example, client side functions to be executed, or MCP servers. Internally hosted tools are within the model provider’s system. For example, OpenAI’s file search or Google Drive integration. The model calls, executes, and retrieves results entirely within the provider's infrastructure, requiring no developer intervention.

Open Responses formalizes the agentic loop which is usually made up of a repeating cycle of reasoning, tool invocation, and response generation that enables models to autonomously complete multi-step tasks.

For internally-hosted tools, the provider manages the entire loop; executing tools, returning results to the model, and streaming output. This means that multi-step workflows like "search documents, summarize findings, then draft an email" use a single request.

Clients control loop behavior via max_tool_calls to cap iterations and tool_choice to constrain which tools are invocable:

The response contains all intermediate items: tool calls, results, reasoning.

Open Responses extends and improves the Responses API, providing richer and more detailed content definitions, compatibility, and deployment options. It also provides a standard way to execute sub-agent loops during primary inference calls, opening up powerful capabilities for AI Applications. We are looking forward to working with the Open Responses team and the community at large on future development of the specification.

You can try Open Responses with Hugging Face Inference Providers today. We have an early access version available for use on Hugging Face Spaces - try it with your Client and Open Responses Compliance Tool today!

Use Open Responses with Hugging Face Inference Providers

#10178. Redmagic 12 Pro review: You’ve never gamed on a phone like this before

The Redmagic 12 Pro impresses with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, liquid cooling, a fan, plus a massive 8,400mAh battery to keep the games going for hours and hours.

As I sat in my living room with my family, playing Monster Hunter Outlanders together on the Redmagic 12 Pro, I completely forgot I was playing on a phone. The game looked perfect. It ran at a locked 60FPS and hadn’t dropped frames since I began playing over an hour ago. It just felt like I was back in college, playing Monster Hunter Freedom on my PSP with my friends in the same room.

Most other phones at this point would have throttled hard. What began at 60FPS almost certainly would have been 40FPS tops after 30 minutes or so; the frame drops during heavy fights would have been even worse, but the Redmagic 12 Pro didn’t skip a beat. Even after a solid hour of playing, the battery had only dropped 10%, completely erasing all concerns about using my phone as a gaming console.

This thing is the real deal, and while I’ve used plenty of high-performance phones and gaming phones over the years, none have quite nailed it as this one has. Now, with my Redmagic 12 Pro and my trusty GameSir G8 Galileo, I can game whenever and wherever I want without battery anxiety or thermal problems. Redmagic has gotten really good at this gaming thing.

Sustained gaming performance is difficult to pull off on a phone, which is why the Redmagic 12 Pro features two types of active cooling: a fan and liquid cooling. This design builds on last year’s with a larger liquid cooling system and a more efficient fan. The intake and exhaust vents are on the sides of the phone, not the back, ensuring these shouldn’t get easily blocked. Despite this, the phone is IP68 and IP69 rated.

Most modern phones have huge camera islands that make them awkward to use in controllers, but the Redmagic 12 Pro features a completely flat build that fits perfectly in *any* controller. I don’t usually like overly flat builds, but it actually suits this phone’s purpose.

This should mean the phone does exceedingly well in benchmarks, but I have the distinct feeling the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 processor inside is making that overly difficult. I don’t have any other SD8 Elite Gen 6 phones just yet, but rumor has it that this is one *hot* chipset. I saw the phone hit 50C during testing, so that definitely seems to be the case.

In 3DMark Solar Bay Extreme, a benchmark that stresses ray-tracing performance over 20 minutes, the Redmagic 12 Pro started at 2065 points and ended at 1169 on its last run. That’s a 43% drop in performance over a 20-minute period, which is in line with passively-cooled phones like the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Regardless, the initial performance is nearly double the S26 Ultra, while the 1169 end score matches the S26 Ultra’s best score and is roughly 35% higher than the S26 Ultra’s sustained performance score of around 860.

Actual gaming seemed to fare better in my testing, where I saw sustained performance consistently outperform any Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone I have in my possession. When running Wanderstop through the phone’s built-in Steam emulation (more on that soon), the Redmagic 12 Pro averaged 72FPS at the highest settings. Other phones with SD8 Elite Gen 5 processors scored half that, at best. Native Android games like Monster Hunter Outlanders worked even better.

But it’s not just performance that sets this phone apart; it’s the gaming features. Redmagic has fully leaned into the mobile gaming power user angle with its software. Pressing and holding the red button on the right side of the phone launches Gravity X, the built-in game launcher that keeps all your games in one place. It even features an embedded Steam emulator, so all you need to do is sign in with your Steam account and download anything in your library.

Overall performance on Steam games is impressive, but like any emulation, not everything is going to work. Hogwarts Legacy worked near-flawlessly at medium settings, but titles like Star Wars Galactic Racer wouldn’t run at all. Other apps that run Steam games, like DroidDeck and Game Native, also work, but the Adreno 850 GPU doesn’t have official support on those apps yet, so compatibility is very hit or miss (mostly miss) for now.

The Redmagic 12 Pro’s in-game menu is also unlike anything you’ve ever seen. It’s not just jam-packed with information, but has a boatload of bespoke features. One custom mapping tool lets you map the triggers (yes, this phone has capacitive triggers on the side) to any on-screen virtual key.

Another utility records all the time, Xbox/PS5/Switch style, and saves a clip at the touch of a floating button. Yet another features on on-screen AI anime character that can interact with your games and even give you gameplay feedback. You can even enable frame gen and Super Resolution in any game. It’s wild.

All this is wrapped up in an incredibly impressive hardware package, with loud, clear speakers, an excellent 185Hz AMOLED display (that uses DC dimming and 2160Hz PWM for eye comfort), with 5,000-nit peak brightness. I measured the actual HDR brightness at 2300-nits, so this can get nice and bright when it needs to.

If there was ever a phone that could play games and still get you through a full day’s normal phone usage, it’s this one. Passthrough charging is also supported, too, so you can keep the battery from getting overcharged or overheated while gaming for hours.

As is the case with many laser-focused devices like this, the camera is the low point of the experience. It’s got a 50MP rear camera and a 50MP ultra wide. Both get the job done, but they’ll never impress you.

The 16MP 9th-generation under display camera looks impressive on the surface — you can’t see it at all, even with light shining off the display — but the results are still far from good. Redmagic uses an AI algorithm to substantially enhance the overall quality, which cleans up the image nicely but exhibits lots of hallucinations. Just look at my eyes in the above picture. It’s not good.

Thankfully, the Android 17-based Redmagic OS 12 software is quite good. Visually, it reminds me of a mix of AOSP and Samsung’s One UI. #10177. How to Create Effective Cold Email Sequences That Generate Replies: A Developer's Guide

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.
