#10106. Transformers.js v4: Now Available on NPM!

We're excited to announce that Transformers.js v4 is now available on NPM! After a year of development (we started in March 2025 🤯), we're finally ready for you to use it.

The biggest change is undoubtedly the adoption of a new WebGPU Runtime, completely rewritten in C++. We've worked closely with the ONNX Runtime team to thoroughly test this runtime across our ~200 supported model architectures, as well as many new v4-exclusive architectures.

In addition to better operator support (for performance, accuracy, and coverage), this new WebGPU runtime allows the same transformers.js code to be used across a wide variety of JavaScript environments, including browsers, server-side runtimes, and desktop applications. That's right, you can now run WebGPU-accelerated models directly in Node, Bun, and Deno!

We've proven that it's possible to run state-of-the-art AI models 100% locally in the browser, and now we're focused on performance: making these models run as fast as possible, even in resource-constrained environments. This required completely rethinking our export strategy, especially for large language models. We achieve this by re-implementing new models operation by operation, leveraging specialized ONNX Runtime Contrib Operators like com.microsoft.GroupQueryAttention, com.microsoft.MatMulNBits, or com.microsoft.QMoE to maximize performance.

For example, adopting the com.microsoft.MultiHeadAttention operator, we were able to achieve a ~4x speedup for BERT-based embedding models.

Developing a new major version gave us the opportunity to invest in the codebase and tackle long-overdue refactoring efforts.

Until now, the GitHub repository served as our npm package. This worked well as long as the repository only exposed a single library. However, looking to the future, we saw the need for various sub-packages that depend heavily on the Transformers.js core while addressing different use cases, like library-specific implementations, or smaller utilities that most users don't need but are essential for some.

That's why we converted the repository to a monorepo using pnpm workspaces. This allows us to ship smaller packages that depend on @huggingface/transformers without the overhead of maintaining separate repositories.

Another major refactoring effort targeted the ever-growing models.js file. In v3, all available models were defined in a single file spanning over 8,000 lines, becoming increasingly difficult to maintain. For v4, we split this into smaller, focused modules with a clear distinction between utility functions, core logic, and model-specific implementations. This new structure improves readability and makes it much easier to add new models. Developers can now focus on model-specific logic without navigating through thousands of lines of unrelated code.

In v3, many Transformers.js example projects lived directly in the main repository. For v4, we've moved them to a dedicated repository, allowing us to maintain a cleaner codebase focused on the core library. This also makes it easier for users to find and contribute to examples without sifting through the main repository.

We updated the Prettier configuration and reformatted all files in the repository. This ensures consistent formatting throughout the codebase, with all future PRs automatically following the same style. No more debates about formatting... Prettier handles it all, keeping the code clean and readable for everyone.

Thanks to our new export strategy and ONNX Runtime's expanding support for custom operators, we've been able to add many new models and architectures to Transformers.js v4. These include popular models like GPT-OSS, Chatterbox, GraniteMoeHybrid, LFM2-MoE, HunYuanDenseV1, Apertus, Olmo3, FalconH1, and Youtu-LLM. Many of these required us to implement support for advanced architectural patterns, including Mamba (state-space models), Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), and Mixture of Experts (MoE). Perhaps most importantly, these models are all compatible with WebGPU, allowing users to run them directly in the browser or server-side JavaScript environments with hardware acceleration. We've released several Transformers.js v4 demos so far... and we'll continue to release more!

We've migrated our build system from Webpack to esbuild, and the results have been incredible. Build times dropped from 2 seconds to just 200 milliseconds, a 10x improvement that makes development iteration significantly faster. Speed isn't the only benefit, though: bundle sizes also decreased by an average of 10% across all builds. The most notable improvement is in transformers.web.js, our default export, which is now 53% smaller, meaning faster downloads and quicker startup times for users.

Version 4 also adds new library features that make it easier to build robust, production-ready applications.

The new ModelRegistry API is designed for production workflows. It provides explicit visibility into pipeline assets before loading anything: list required files with get_pipeline_files, inspect per-file metadata with get_file_metadata (quite useful to calculate total download size), check cache status with is_pipeline_cached, and clear cached artifacts with clear_pipeline_cache. You can also query available precision types for a model with get_available_dtypes. Based on this new API, progress_callback now includes a progress_total event, making it easy to render end-to-end loading progress without manually aggregating per-file updates.

We also added new environment controls for model loading. env.useWasmCache enables caching of WASM runtime files (when cache storage is available), allowing applications to work fully offline after the initial load.

env.fetch lets you provide a custom fetch implementation for use cases such as authenticated model access, custom headers, and abortable requests.

Finally, logging is easier to manage in real-world deployments. ONNX Runtime WebGPU warnings are now hidden by default, and you can set explicit verbosity levels for both Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime. This update, also driven by community feedback, keeps console output focused on actionable signals rather than low-value noise.

A frequent request from users was to extract the tokenization logic into a separate library, and with v4, that's exactly what we've done. @huggingface/tokenizers is a complete refactor of the tokenization logic, designed to work seamlessly across browsers and server-side runtimes. At just 8.8kB (gzipped) with zero dependencies, it's incredibly lightweight while remaining fully type-safe.

This separation keeps the core of Transformers.js focused and lean while offering a versatile, standalone tool that any WebML project can use independently.

We've made several quality-of-life improvements across the library. The type system has been enhanced with dynamic pipeline types that adapt based on inputs, providing better developer experience and type safety.

Additionally, we've added support for larger models exceeding 8B parameters. In our tests, we've been able to run GPT-OSS 20B (q4f16) at ~60 tokens per second on an M4 Pro Max.

We want to extend our heartfelt thanks to everyone who contributed to this major release, especially the ONNX Runtime team for their incredible work on the new WebGPU runtime and their support throughout development, as well as all external contributors and early testers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just over a year ago, T-Mobile launched its home fiber internet service in the United States, buoyed by its acquisition of Lumos. At the time, T-Mobile’s fiber service reached half a million customers across the country, with speeds of up to 2 Gbps. This week, T-Mobile introduced a new 5 Gbps tier for customers who crave even more speed.

The 5 Gbps tier is priced at $90 per month and comes with a 10-year price guarantee. Given how often legacy cable internet providers would raise prices, forcing customers to jump through hoops to keep the status quo, a 10-year price lock could be very appealing to a large segment of the population. But as with most things, there is some fine print to the offer, which reads, “Taxes & fees, voluntary equipment or speed upgrades, select limited-time promotions, per-use charges, third-party services, and network management practices aren’t included.”

To get the $90/month price, you’ll also need to set up AutoPay with T-Mobile. However, to further sweeten the deal, customers will also receive a mesh Wi-Fi extender that broadens the coverage of the included Fiber gateway.

For new customers, T-Mobile is also offering two months of free service (via bill credits) and a $300 virtual prepaid debit card. T-Mobile’s pricing for the 5 Gbps plan is an aggressive deal in the home fiber market. For example, GFiber (Google) costs $100/month for 3 Gbps speeds, while the company’s 8 Gbps tier is $150/month.

T-Mobile’s new 5 Gbps plan joins the existing 2 Gbps ($70/month), 1 Gbps ($60/month), and 300 Mbps ($45/month) plans. All of the plans feature symmetrical upload/download speeds, which is a big upgrade for anyone coming from a traditional cable internet provider.

For people who don’t have access to T-Mobile’s growing fiber footprint in the U.S., the company also offers its unlimited 5G Home Internet service, with prices starting at $50/month.

Google Home is one of the most user-friendly smart home ecosystems, and Google has built out an extensive collection of cameras, speakers, and displays. That positions them as great gifts to expand someone’s smart home.

It’s pretty common to get one or two smart home devices and call it a day, but ecosystems like Google Home begin to come alive when there are several devices working in harmony with each other. For instance, you can start out with the Google Nest Learning Thermostat (4th gen), as many do. It makes A/C and heat controls easy, and even saves you money along the way.

But adding something like the Google Home Speaker with Gemini built-in means you get even more control of your home’s indoor environment. You could go a step further and add a Google Nest Cam (indoor or outdoor) or a Google Nest Doorbell, whether wired or battery. It’s a bit pricier, but I love the Google Nest Cam with Floodlight as a smart home gift option for someone, since it provides more utility.

In any case, adding a couple more foundational pieces to your smart home makes it more useful. And as Google adds features with Gemini for Home, users get access to smart alerts and notifications that those cameras didn’t provide a year or two ago, all within the Google Home app.

If you’re gifting for someone who doesn’t have the beginnings of a smart home setup, Google’s Nest products are a good start. You could start with the Google Home Speaker, depending on their needs. If they like listening to music and want a smart home assistant at the ready, Google’s latest speaker delivers.

The Google Home Speaker has a 360-degree speaker that throws audio in every direction, filling the room. It controls other devices as that smart home fills out, and it can even act as part of a stereo setup for the Google TV Streamer.

Right now, the Google Home Speaker is at its lowest price on Best Buy, sitting at $79.99 – $20 off. It comes in some great colorways, too, like Berry and Jade. Of course, there’s Porcelain and Hazel for more toned-down looks.

Another great smart home starter gift is the Nest Learning Thermostat (4th gen) or Nest Thermostat. The difference between the two comes down to look and capabilities, but both work very well.

The Nest Learning Thermostat (4th gen) works with the majority of HVAC systems and converts them into one manageable system through the Google Home app. Over time, it learns your heating and cooling habits to form better schedules that save you money and stress.

Right now, the Nest Learning Thermostat (4th) gen is down to $219 from $279 at Best Buy – $60 off. That’s the best price we’ve seen from the store, and it’s a good deal overall.

Best Buy is also offering a couple of bundles if you want to go further. You can add Nest Cams to your cart with the Nest Learning Thermostat for $100 off the order. If you want to bundle a couple of items into a gift for someone –or yourself – that’s the way to go.

Of course, you can’t go wrong with the Nest Doorbell cameras (wired or battery). Go for the battery edition if you’re limited on wiring options or want to use it at an apartment. Wired is the better choice for homes, since it makes 24/7 recording possible for more security.

You can also check out Best Buy’s other offers on Google’s smart home products. It might be worth bookmarking as deals appear during Black Friday.

#10102. OpenEnv in Practice: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents in Real-World Environments

AI agents often perform impressively in controlled research settings, yet struggle when deployed in real-world systems where they must reason across multiple steps, interact with real tools and APIs, operate under partial information, and recover from errors in stateful, permissioned environments—highlighting a persistent gap between research success and production reliability.

OpenEnv is an open-source framework from Meta and Hugging Face designed to address this challenge by standardizing how agents interact with real environments. As part of this collaboration, Turing contributed a production-grade calendar management environment to study tool-using agents under realistic constraints such as access control, temporal reasoning, and multi-agent coordination.

In this post, we explore how OpenEnv works in practice, why calendars serve as a powerful benchmark for real-world agent evaluation, and what our findings reveal about the current limitations of tool-using agents.

OpenEnv is a framework for evaluating AI agents against real systems rather than simulations. It provides a standardized way to connect agents to real tools and workflows while preserving the structure needed for consistent and reliable evaluation.

OpenEnv uses a gym-oriented API (reset, step, action, observations) like OpenAI's Gymnasium. Also, OpenEnv uses a standard MCP tool call interface to connect to envs which provides a consistent interface across domains and simulation to production environments.

The environments maintain state across multiple actions—enabling long-horizon reasoning—and can connect directly to real APIs and tools such as browsers, code repositories, or calendars. This shifts evaluation from "Can this work in a controlled demo?" to "Can this operate reliably in the real world?"

Calendar systems are deceptively complex. While scheduling a meeting seems simple, real-world calendar management requires agents to reason over time, permissions, multiple users, and incomplete information—often across several dependent steps. These properties make calendars a powerful testbed for evaluating tool-using agents outside controlled simulations.

To ground OpenEnv in this kind of realistic, demanding use case, Turing built a production-grade calendar management environment referred to as the Calendar Gym. Rather than simulating scheduling in the abstract, it exposes agents to the same constraints they would face in real calendar systems: Access Control Lists across users and calendars, limited visibility into other users' state, and multi-step workflows where actions must be chained in the correct order. Agents interact with a rich set of calendar operations—from listing calendars to modifying events and permissions—and must handle failed actions, incorrect assumptions, and missing permissions. Each session runs in an isolated environment, enabling reliable comparisons across runs.

Below is a code example of how to use the Calendar Gym. We explore the environment, discover available tools, list calendars, create an event, and print the result.

Below is an excerpt of what the Calendar Gym returns when you call ListToolsAction. Each entry includes the tool name plus an input schema (what arguments the tool accepts).

Evaluating agents in the Calendar Gym revealed consistent patterns which were common across multiple domains. While agents often perform well on individual game like actions, reliability breaks down as tasks become longer, more ambiguous, and more constrained.

Multi-step reasoning is the primary bottleneck. Agents struggle to correctly chain actions across longer workflows, suggesting that benchmarks need to test sustained reasoning over multiple dependent steps—not just single tool calls.

Ambiguity significantly degrades performance. Agents achieved close to 90% success on tasks with explicit calendar identifiers, but success dropped to roughly 40% when the same tasks were phrased using natural language descriptions. Building stronger lookup and validation into agent loops—rather than relying on the LLM to resolve references unaided—appears essential.

Correct tool choice isn't enough. Across failed interactions, more than half of errors stemmed from malformed tool arguments or incorrect ordering, even when the right tool was selected. Reliable agent behavior depends as much on execution quality and structured feedback as on tool selection—environment design matters.

These challenges are not unique to scheduling and calendars. They reflect broader limitations that emerge whenever agents operate in changing systems over long periods of time, and they point toward evaluation frameworks that test permissions, partial observability, and multi-step workflows together.

OpenEnv provides a foundation for testing agents under realistic conditions, and the Calendar Gym demonstrates how seemingly simple domains can surface deep challenges in reasoning, ambiguity resolution, and tool use. By evaluating agents where failure is measurable and constraints are real, we gain clearer insight into what it takes to build agents that operate reliably in production.

For a deeper dive into the Calendar Gym's design, benchmarking methodology, and quantitative results, explore the full technical article on Turing's site. To explore a clone of the Calendar Gym, visit the Calendar Gym space.

In practice, tool integrations rarely fail in dramatic ways; they fail in small, predictable ones. When wiring up MCP tools to real APIs (like calendar operations), we encountered a handful of recurring issues.

Below are three common failure modes we’ve seen in production, along with representative error payloads and mitigation strategies. These examples illustrate not just what can go wrong, but how structured errors can help agents recover gracefully.

The agent calls a valid tool (e.g. events_insert), but the arguments do not match the declared JSON schema.

We can mitigate this by providing one canonical example of a correct 'events_insert' call in your prompt. Return structured validation errors so the model can repair and retry instead of failing silently.

The tool call is syntactically correct, but the API rejects it due to insufficient permissions.

We can mitigate this by clearly documenting the required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call. Clearly document required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call.

The event is rejected by the API, or it is created at an unexpected time.

We can mitigate this by standardizing on RFC3339 with explicit timezone offsets (e.g. 2026-02-11T09:30:00-05:00). Include at least one correct datetime example in your documentation to anchor model behavior and reduce repair retries.

The death of physical games could be getting closer as Macronix, one of Nintendo’s key ROM chip suppliers for Switch and Switch 2 game cartridges, is reportedly shutting down its ROM business to focus on manufacturing NOR and NAND flash chips to supply data centers, multiple reports claim. Storage is already becoming expensive, and Macronix’s move may force Nintendo to increase cartridge prices, produce more Game-Key cards, or lean more towards digital purchases.

"Nintendo's main memory chip maker is quitting the Switch business," MST Financial David Gibson reports on X. "Macronix, which makes the ROM chips in Switch 1 and Switch 2 game memory cards, is phasing out that business. There will be no new ROM products, and Q3 is the last quarter it reports ROM sales separately.

1/4 Nintendo's main memory chip maker is quitting the Switch business Macronix, which makes the ROM chips in Switch 1 and Switch 2 game memory cards, is phasing out that business. There will be no new ROM products, and Q3 is the last quarter it reports ROM sales separately.November 4, 2026

He notes that Macronix ROM sales in Q3 of this year dropped to 5%, compared to last year’s 26%. Furthermore, Gibson says that the NT$37.8 billion capital expenditure is allocated to NOR and NAND Flash, leaving none for ROM as the company shifts its manufacturing capacity to supply AI needs — Taipei Times corroborated the report, stating, "At the same time, Macronix is gradually phasing out of ROM production, Wu said. It also reports that Macronix’s capital expenditure is split into two phases, the NT$ 22 billion for expanding manufacturing capacity, followed by an additional NT$15.8 billion for NAND flash used in eMMCs and 3D NAND.

Gibson expects that Nintendo’s digital margins will grow through more Game-Key Cards or digital-only sales, but as Macronix isn’t the only source of ROM chips, “physical cards will likely carry on for some time.” Gibson further reports that digital margins have been slowly rising, with numbers fluctuating depending on the quarter due to major physical game launches.

3/4 My view: Macronix isn't Nintendo's only game memory card maker, so physical cards will likely carry on for some time. But at the margin, digital will grow, through more Game-Key Cards (which hold a download key, not the game) and digital-only sales.November 4, 2026

ROHM group companies ROHM Semiconductor and LAPIS Semiconductor still supply ROM chips to Nintendo, so it’s unlikely that Nintendo will eventually go digital-only in the near future like Sony and Microsoft’s recent plans. With one less supplier, however, Nintendo may be forced to increase prices on physical games.

The biggest loser in all of this (besides the gamers), however, may be fabless chip design company MegaChips. Nintendo doesn’t buy ROM chips from Macronix directly; MegaChips designs the ROM chips according to Nintendo’s needs and, having no manufacturing capacity, outsources it to Macronix. MegaChips’ 2022 company report states that Nintendo accounted for 87.8% of its sales, while Macronix accounted for 67.8% of its outsourced manufacturing purchases. The report even states that if Macronix could manufacture ROM chips, “MegaChips’ operating results may be impacted.” The 2022 document further says that there was no sign that the risk would become apparent; however, the risk just became very real, and we’re not aware of MegaChips’ contingency plan to deal with this situation. However, Macronix and MegaChips have likely talked amongst themselves about Macronix’s plans to stop ROM chip manufacturing, and have given MegaChips some time to find another manufacturer before Macronix shuts down the ROM chip business.

#10100. 'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

An ongoing supply chain attack is harvesting credentials and sensitive data from thousands of developer repositories.

An ongoing attack is abusing compromised GitHub tokens to harvest cloud secrets and credentials from thousands of developer repositories, bringing into focus how compromised developer accounts can provide a gateway into enterprise cloud environments.

Dubbed "Gheist," the campaign has left more than 13,500 malicious branches — or versions of a project's code — across more than 850 compromised GitHub accounts, according to a report published over the weekend by Wiz Research.

The campaign affects everything from personal projects to private enterprise repositories, although public repositories are protected by safeguards GitHub introduced in July, according to the report.

"The control GitHub added is focused on protecting public repositories from workflow abuse vectors," Wiz researcher Rami McCarthy tells Dark Reading. However, "once an enterprise credential is compromised, that control doesn’t apply," he adds.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Wiz also found overlap between Gheist-affected GitHub accounts and other abuse campaigns, including repository-based malware distribution, attempts to exploit GitHub Actions for computing resources, and possible infections linked to other malware operations.

This overlap — which distinguishes Gheist from similar campaigns — suggests stolen developer tokens may be reused or shared among threat actors, "demonstrating the complexity and activity of this threat landscape," McCarthy says.

The campaign relies on a workflow named "sync-check," which is committed to each repository accessible through a stolen token, the researchers wrote.

"The workflow seeks to print the repository’s secrets into its own workflow log," they wrote. "Then, the tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later. The tool's API requests carry the user agent 'gheist,' which gives the campaign its name."

Wiz began tracking the activity Sept. 15 and said the operation remains active and evolving as of Oct. 24. The researchers reported the activity to GitHub, and about two-thirds of the implicated accounts are no longer available, which "likely indicates response activity," according to the report.

The tokens appear to have come primarily from two sources: infostealer malware and credentials exposed in earlier software supply chain compromises, the researchers noted.

GitHub tokens authorize users and applications to access repositories, code, and administrative functions, making them valuable to attackers seeking to compromise projects and organizations.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

Gheist uses stolen GitHub tokens to create branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters. The attackers then add the GitHub Actions workflow at .github/workflows/sync-check.yml, using the commit message "ci: sync config," according to the report.

"The commit is unsigned and authored as the token's owner," the researchers wrote. The resulting push event triggers a workflow that attempts to print environment variables and repository secrets into its log. The attack encodes the output using Base32 before retrieving the logs through the GitHub API and deleting the workflow run seconds later.

"Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block," the researchers explained.

A key finding is that Wiz observed successful attacks in private repositories and enterprise environments, where the public-repository safeguard did not apply. Most GitHub-targeted activity, by contrast, primarily affects public repositories, McCarthy tells Dark Reading.

"The attack succeeded in the environments organizations considered safest because a credential issued to a human months ago still carried full write authority," says James Matchett, head of security at supply chain security firm Cloudsmith, in an email interview. "'Private' is not a control. Scoped, short-lived credentials, a tight inventory of what can push and pull, and the discipline to rotate after every incident are the control.”

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

Wiz observed the attackers cycling through tokens belonging to multiple users and automation accounts, and cloning private repositories before planting malicious workflows. Within hours, cloud credentials from the same organization were used to enumerate AWS Secrets Manager, the researchers added.

Wiz estimates that the campaign affected "on the scale of a dozen companies," McCarthy says. However, "we have not seen consistent or automated abuse outside of mass cloning of GitHub repositories and the core credential theft," he says.

Token abuse is an increasingly common way for attackers to infiltrate organizations through the developer pipeline. Research presented at Black Hat Europe last year found that some of the most significant software supply chain incidents over the preceding year involved threat actors exploiting GitHub flaws. Defenders therefore must treat developer projects as critical organizational assets.

To defend against Gheist and other forms of token abuse, Wiz urged security teams to hunt for malicious GitHub Actions workflows, rotate exposed secrets, and treat compromised self-hosted runners as potential infrastructure breaches.

More specifically, defenders should look for branches named "ci-sync-" followed by six characters, where the only change is a new .github/workflows/sync-check.yml file with the commit message "ci: sync config," the researchers advised. Administrators also should review GitHub audit logs for workflow runs on "ci-sync-*" branches that were deleted within a minute of completion, as well as activity from the user agent "gheist."

For broader protection against GitHub token abuse, Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at security firm Secure.com, recommends that organizations "replace long-lived personal access tokens with GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens" and "require reviewers on any environment that holds production secrets." These measures can help limit attackers' ability to access sensitive credentials even if they obtain valid tokens.

#10099. How to Optimize AI-Generated Images for Faster Websites

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI-generated images are becoming a common part of modern web development. Developers use them for website banners, product illustrations, landing pages, blog posts, and digital interfaces. However, generating an image is only one part of the process. Before publishing it, developers need to ensure that the image loads quickly, displays correctly across devices, and maintains its visual quality.

Large image files can increase page size, consume unnecessary bandwidth, and delay the appearance of important content. These problems can affect user experience and website performance, particularly on mobile devices and slower internet connections.

A reliable image optimization workflow helps address these challenges. By selecting appropriate dimensions, choosing efficient image formats, automating image processing, and implementing responsive delivery, developers can improve loading performance without sacrificing visual quality.

This guide explains how to optimize AI-generated images using practical techniques and development tools.

Images often account for a significant portion of a webpage's total download size. Uploading large, unoptimized images can make pages slower and increase the amount of data visitors need to download.

Several common problems contribute to poor image performance:

Incorrect dimensions waste bandwidth on smaller screens.

Missing image dimensions can cause unexpected layout shifts.

Poor responsive configuration can make browsers download unnecessarily large images.

Incorrect loading priorities can delay important visual content.

These issues can affect Core Web Vitals, including Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), which measures how quickly the largest visible content element appears.

For developers, image optimization should therefore be part of the website development workflow rather than a final task performed immediately before publication.

Before optimizing an image, determine where it will appear on the website. A full-width banner requires different dimensions from a product thumbnail or a small interface graphic.

For example, a website might use the following dimensions:

These dimensions are examples rather than fixed requirements. The appropriate size depends on the website layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

When preparing source visuals, developers can explore different AI image generation options and consider how the generated images will fit their intended layouts.

Once the image is ready, keep a high-quality master file. This allows developers to create smaller versions for different screen sizes without repeatedly compressing an already optimized image.

Avoid enlarging small images unnecessarily because upscaling can introduce blur and visible artifacts.

Choosing the right format can reduce image size while preserving acceptable visual quality.

Three commonly used formats are AVIF, WebP, and JPEG.

AVIF: Often provides efficient compression for photographs and detailed illustrations. It can significantly reduce file sizes, although encoding may take longer.

WebP: Supports lossy and lossless compression, transparency, and animation. It offers broad browser support and is suitable for many website images.

JPEG: Remains useful for photographs and situations where compatibility with older software or systems is important.

PNG is appropriate for certain lossless graphics, screenshots, and images that require transparency. However, it can produce unnecessarily large files when used for photographic content.

No format is automatically the best choice for every image. Developers should compare file sizes and inspect visual quality before selecting the final output.

A practical approach is to generate AVIF and WebP versions and provide a JPEG fallback where necessary.

Manually resizing and converting images becomes time-consuming when a website contains dozens or hundreds of visual assets.

Automation makes the process more consistent. Developers can use Sharp, a Node.js image-processing library, to resize images, convert formats, and generate multiple versions from a single source file.

Next, create a file named build-images.mjs:

The script creates multiple image sizes in both WebP and AVIF formats.

The quality settings are starting points, not universal recommendations. Developers should adjust them after checking the resulting file sizes and visual details.

This approach is particularly useful for content-heavy websites, product catalogs, and applications that publish images regularly.

Responsive image delivery allows browsers to select an appropriate image based on the visitor's screen and the space available in the layout.

HTML provides two important attributes for this purpose: srcset and sizes.

The srcset attribute lists the available image files and their widths. The sizes attribute describes how wide the image is expected to appear at different viewport sizes.

In this example, the image is expected to occupy approximately 720 pixels on wider screens and nearly the full viewport width on smaller screens.

The browser uses this information to choose an appropriate image candidate.

One common mistake is setting sizes="100vw" for an image that occupies only a small part of the page. This can encourage the browser to download a larger file than necessary.

Always ensure that the sizes attribute reflects the actual website layout.

The HTML picture element allows developers to provide multiple image formats and a fallback option.

The browser selects a supported format, while the img element provides the fallback image and alternative text.

Developers should verify that every referenced file exists and that its dimensions match the intended layout.

The picture element can also support different crops for desktop and mobile devices. This is useful when a wide banner needs a separate composition for smaller screens.

Images without defined dimensions can cause content to move while the browser loads the file. This behavior contributes to Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

Including width and height attributes helps browsers reserve the appropriate space before the image finishes loading.

For responsive layouts, developers can use CSS:

This allows images to scale within their containers while maintaining their proportions.

Images below the initial viewport can generally use native lazy loading:

However, the main hero image should not normally be lazy-loaded when it is responsible for LCP. Delaying an important above-the-fold image can make the page appear slower.

Where appropriate, developers can use fetchpriority="high" for the main image to help the browser prioritize its download.

The correct strategy depends on the image's position and importance within the page.

Image optimization involves more than file size and dimensions. Developers should also consider accessibility, file organization, and metadata.

Alternative text helps people using screen readers understand meaningful images. It should describe the image's purpose in the context of the page.

Decorative images that provide no useful information should generally use an empty alt attribute.

File names should also be descriptive. Names such as home-office-sunrise.webp are easier to understand and maintain than generic names such as image-final-v3.png.

Metadata requires additional consideration. Image-processing tools may remove metadata by default to reduce file size. This can include information that a project needs to preserve, depending on its requirements.

Before removing metadata, developers should review whether the website or client requires attribution, provenance information, or other embedded details.

After implementing an optimization workflow, test the actual website rather than relying only on exported file sizes.

Chrome DevTools provides useful information about image requests.

Open Developer Tools and select the Network panel.

Resize the viewport or use device emulation.

Check whether the browser downloads appropriately sized images.

Developers can also inspect the image selected by the browser through the console:

This returns the current image URL selected for that element.

For websites with multiple images, inspect the relevant elements individually.

Finally, run an audit using Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights. These tools can identify issues involving oversized images, image formats, loading priorities, and other performance factors.

Image optimization is only one part of website performance. Server response times, caching, CSS, JavaScript, and third-party scripts can also influence loading speed.

Several mistakes can reduce the effectiveness of an image optimization workflow:

Uploading original images without checking their dimensions.

Assuming one format always produces the smallest file.

Omitting the sizes attribute from responsive images.

Lazy-loading important above-the-fold images.

Applying excessive compression and damaging visual details.

Removing metadata without checking project requirements.

Measuring file size without inspecting the final visual quality.

A consistent testing process helps identify these issues before they affect visitors.

Four to six sizes may be sufficient for many websites. The ideal number depends on the layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

Yes. Reducing the size of the main content image, providing responsive versions, and avoiding unnecessary loading delays can improve LCP when that image is the largest contentful element.

No. Lazy loading is useful for images outside the initial viewport. Important images near the top of the page should generally load promptly.

The fundamental techniques are the same as those used for conventional images. However, AI-generated visuals may contain complex textures, gradients, and fine details that require careful inspection after compression.

AI-generated images can improve website design and make it easier to create custom visual content. However, efficient delivery requires more than exporting an image and uploading it to a website.

Developers should choose suitable dimensions, compare modern image formats, automate processing, and implement responsive image delivery. Including image dimensions helps prevent layout shifts, while appropriate loading priorities can improve the experience for visitors.

By testing images across different devices and reviewing their actual performance, development teams can maintain visual quality while reducing unnecessary downloads.

A repeatable optimization workflow makes it easier to publish new visuals without sacrificing website speed, accessibility, or reliability.

#10097. Custom Kernels for All from Codex and Claude

tl;dr: We built an agent skill that teaches coding agents how to write production CUDA kernels. Then we pointed Claude and Codex at two real targets: a diffusers pipeline and a transformers model. The agents produced working kernels for both, with correct PyTorch bindings and benchmarks, end to end.

Writing CUDA kernels is hard. Writing CUDA kernels that correctly integrate with transformers and diffusers is harder. There are architecture-specific memory access patterns, vectorization strategies, warp shuffle reductions, and a dozen integration pitfalls that trip up even experienced developers. It is exactly the kind of specialized, high-stakes problem where agent skills shine.

We gave coding agents the domain knowledge they need, like which GPU architecture to target, how to structure a kernel-builder project, when to use shared memory versus registers, and how to write PyTorch bindings. The agents did the rest. If you have used the LLM training skill or read We Got Claude to Teach Open Models, the pattern will feel familiar: package domain expertise into a skill, point the agent at a problem, and let it work.

The Kernel Hub solved the distribution of custom hardware kernels. You can load pre-compiled kernels from the Hub with a single get_kernel call. No builds, no flags. However, someone still needs to write the kernels. That is the gap this skill fills.

CUDA kernel development has a brutal surface area:

This is domain knowledge that gets lost in documentation tabs and Stack Overflow answers. An agent skill packages it into context that loads on demand.

First, let's show how to use the skill right away, then we'll dive into the details of how we benchmarked the kernels.

The skill ships with the kernels library. Install it into your coding agent with a single command:

This drops the skill into .claude/skills/cuda-kernels/ where Claude Code and Cursor pick it up automatically. For other agents:

Or, you can go for something more open-ended:

The agent can read the skill, select the right architecture parameters, generate the CUDA source, write the PyTorch bindings, set up build.toml, and create a benchmark script.

If you're working on more complex kernels, or architecture-specific optimizations, that aren't covered in the skill, then the skill supplies the fundamental building blocks and patterns to get you started. We are also open to contributions on the skill itself.

The skill is roughly 550 tokens of structured guidance plus reference scripts, GPU optimization guides, troubleshooting docs, and complete working examples. Agentic coding tools like Codex and Claude can read this and produce a working kernel project.

When an agent loads this, it gets everything it needs to go from "write me an RMSNorm kernel" to a buildable, benchmarkable project. It will grep and glob the skill to find the relevant files and directories. So it's important to structure the skill in a way that is easy to find.

The agent is instructed to generate kernels that conform to the templates in references/kernel-templates.md and produce a complete kernel project:

The agent built RMSNorm, RoPE 3D, GEGLU, and AdaLN kernels for LTX-Video, a video generation pipeline from diffusers. The full example is at examples/ltx_video/. We optimized the RMSNorm kernel for H100. Both benchmarks were run on H100 80GB HBM3 at precision BFloat16.

If you want to check out the generated kernel, got to this example

First, we compare the isolated RMSNorm kernel performance against the PyTorch baseline. This is the main speedup in the optimized pipeline.

Average speedup: 1.88x and a bandwidth efficiency: 34.7% of H100 theoretical (3,350 GB/s)

Next, we compare the end-to-end video generation performance of the optimized kernels against the baseline (no compile) and the torch.compile baseline.

RMSNorm accounts for ~5% of total compute in LTX-Video. The remaining time is spent in attention, linear projections, and VAE decode. The 6% end-to-end speedup from a single kernel type is consistent with that profile.

The agent built an RMSNorm kernel for Qwen3-8B, a large language model from transformers with 65 RMSNorm modules across 32 layers. The full example is at examples/qwen3_8b/. We optimized the RMSNorm kernel for H100. Both benchmarks were run on H100 80GB HBM3 at precision BFloat16.

If you want to explore the kernel, check it out here.

Once again, we compare the isolated RMSNorm kernel performance against the PyTorch baseline.

Average speedup: 1.94x and a bandwidth efficiency: 22.3% of H100 theoretical (3,350 GB/s)

Speedup scales with sequence length: 1.58x at 128 tokens, 2.47x at 8192 tokens. For long-context inference, the custom kernel roughly halves RMSNorm latency.

The agent gives you a working kernel. The Kernel Hub lets you share it so anyone can load it without compilation. Here is the full path from agent output to published kernel.

The agent produces a project that already follows the kernel-builder layout:

The build.toml tells kernel-builder what to build. The agent generates this for you, including the correct cuda-capabilities for your target GPU:

Kernel Hub kernels must support all recent PyTorch and CUDA configurations. The kernel-builder Nix flake handles this automatically. Copy the example flake.nix into your project and run:

This builds the kernel for every required PyTorch/CUDA variant and places the results in build/. For faster builds, enable the HuggingFace Nix cache:

Create a model repo on the Hub and upload the built kernel:

Once published, anyone can use your kernel with zero compilation:

get_kernel detects the user's Python, PyTorch, and CUDA versions and downloads the matching pre-compiled binary. No builds, no flags, typically ready in seconds.

The skill and the Hub are complementary. The skill handles development. The Hub handles distribution. Build a kernel with the skill, validate it with the benchmark scripts, publish it to the Hub, and it becomes a one-liner for everyone else.

We built an agent skill that teaches coding agents how to write production CUDA kernels. Then we pointed Claude and Codex at two real targets: a diffusers pipeline and a transformers model. The agents produced working kernels for both, with correct PyTorch bindings and benchmarks, end to end. We benchmarked the kernels and found that the optimized kernels can provide a speedup in both isolated and end-to-end performance.

Installation with pip install kernels works, but the command has no skills option:

The kernels repo has kernels-builder and the kernels library.

This is the reason why doing a pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/kernels.git would not work.

Question: Is the baseline in section Isolated RMSNorm benchmark (Pytorch baseline) using torch.compile() or not? Custom kernels should be ideally beating torch.compiled code.

Mio took Shipaton’s Grand Prize, with RevenueCat highlighting its revenue and growth in a crowded habit-tracking market.

Clucky’s rooster is determined to get you out of bed. Turning off an alarm can require solving a problem, moving around, or finding an object, bringing a little friction to the temptation to snooze.

Put a few phones on the table, and Bubble Games turns their screens into a shared game board. Objects move between devices as friends compete in minigames, including a virtual hot potato.

Its HAMM Award win recognizes how the business model fits the game: a shared Credits currency connects rewarded ads, optional packs, and a subscription, while core modes remain free. Players can choose the option that fits how often they play.

Just Add begins with a craving. Type what you feel like eating, describe it aloud, or take a photo, and the app suggests three meals built around it, adding protein, fiber, and healthy fats to round out the plate.

Shopping support, hands-free cooking, and remembered preferences help carry the idea through to dinner. The winner of Abbey’s Kitchen’s nutrition challenge also impressed judges with a dinner-host feature that accounts for other people’s preferences.

Friendpire won the separate Conflict of Interest Award, which was open to RevenueCat and sponsor employees and judged by Shipaton participants. It is included here as an optional sidebar and is not part of the 20 first-place count above.

From a useful tool for the workday to a game for your next night in, Shipaton’s winners show how much can come from taking an idea all the way to a shipped app. Explore the winners above, or browse RevenueCat’s full announcement for more apps from the competition.

#10094. How to Test AI-Generated Content Before It Reaches Your Users

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most teams now ship something an AI helped write: help-center articles, product descriptions, release notes, even code comments. The draft appears in seconds, and that speed is the trap. Nobody tests it the way they would test a new feature, so mistakes slip through that a quick review would have caught.

This guide is about the other side of AI testing. Instead of using AI to test your software, you test what AI hands you. Here is a simple routine that fits into a normal publishing or release process.

AI writing sounds confident whether or not it is right. A model can invent a statistic (researchers call this hallucination and have documented it across many text-generation systems), quote a feature your product does not have, or describe a setting that was renamed two releases ago. The sentence reads smoothly, so the error hides in plain sight.

Traditional QA does not cover this. A unit test tells you the page loads. It says nothing about whether the claim on the page is true. That gap is where most AI-related incidents begin.

1. Define what "good" means before you generate anything. Write down the audience, the claims you are willing to make and the sources you trust. A short brief makes the output easier to judge, because you are comparing it with something concrete.

2. Check every factual claim. Highlight each number, name and statement of fact, then verify it against a primary source. Google's own guidance on generative AI content tells publishers to fact-check AI output, including titles, descriptions and alt text, before publishing. If you cannot confirm a claim in a minute or two, cut it or rewrite it as something you can support.

3. Test the instructions. For tutorials and how-to content, follow the steps exactly as written on a clean machine or account. Commands that fail and menus that no longer exist show up immediately this way.

4. Review the voice. Replace vague phrases with specifics from your own experience: a real customer question, a real error message, a real number from your analytics. This is also what separates useful content from filler.

5. Keep a human owner. Every piece should have a named person who approved it. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework makes the same point at organization level: people stay accountable for how AI is used and evaluated. If something goes wrong later, you know who to ask and where to fix it.

Some teams also run drafts through an AI detector. That can be useful as a prompt for a closer look, for example when freelancers or vendors deliver work and you want to know how much of it was machine-generated. A high score is a reason to read more carefully. It is not proof of anything, and it should never decide an outcome on its own, because detectors make mistakes in both directions. A Stanford study found that GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers, and short texts are easy to misjudge too. If you want a quick second opinion on a draft, a tool like Tester AI can give you a starting point for that conversation.

Review works best when it is not optional. A few small habits make it stick.

Treating the first draft as finished. It is a starting point. Plan time for review the same way you plan time for writing.

Reviewing for grammar only. Clean sentences are not evidence of correct content. Check meaning first and polish second.

Letting the tool grade its own work. Asking the same model to confirm its answer rarely catches real errors. Use a source or a person.

Skipping legal and brand review. Generated text can echo existing material or make promises your company cannot keep. Anything customer-facing deserves a second pair of eyes.

AI can save hours of drafting, but speed only helps if the result is trustworthy. Treat generated content like code from a new contributor: useful, often good, and always reviewed before it goes live. A short routine of defining quality, verifying facts, testing instructions and keeping a human owner will catch most problems before your users do.

Do I need to test AI-generated content if a human edits it? Yes. Editing for style does not confirm that the facts are correct. Verify claims separately from polishing the wording.

How long should a review take? For a typical article, expect roughly the time it takes to read it twice plus a few minutes per factual claim. Reviews are faster when the brief and sources are prepared in advance.

Can an AI detector prove that text was written by a machine? No. Detectors estimate likelihood, and they can be wrong. Use the result as a signal for human review, never as the final decision.

What should I check first? Start with numbers, names, dates and anything a customer could act on, such as prices, steps or legal statements. Those carry the highest risk if they are wrong.

#10093. One-Shot Any Web App with Gradio's gr.HTML

Gradio 6 quietly shipped a very powerful feature: gr.HTML now supports custom templates, scoped CSS, and JavaScript interactivity. Which means you can build pretty much any web component — and Claude (or any other frontier LLM) can generate the whole thing in one shot: frontend, backend, and state management, all in a single Python file.

We tested this by building different types of apps. Each one is a single Python file, no build step, deployable to Hugging Face Spaces in seconds.

Pomodoro Timer: A focus timer where a pixel-art tree grows as you work. Starts as a seed, sprouts branches, grows leaves. Complete a session and the tree joins your forest. Session tracking, theme switching, break modes — all interactive, all in one file.

The tree animation alone would normally require a separate React component. Here it's just CSS keyframes in css_template and state updates in js_on_load.

GitHub Contribution Heatmap: Click any cell to toggle contributions. Multiple color themes. Pattern generators (streaks, seasonal, random). Live stats that update as you edit.

Kanban Board: Full drag-and-drop between columns. Inline editing (double-click any card). Search feature that can filter in real-time. Collapsible columns.

Drag-and-drop usually means pulling in a library. Here it's native HTML5 drag events wired up in js_on_load, with state synced back to Python via trigger('change').

Spin-to-Win Wheel: Smooth CSS animation, rotation state that persists across re-renders. Preset configurations for yes/no decisions, restaurant picking, team selection. You can also add custom spinning segments on the fly.

This is where gr.HTML gets really interesting for ML work: you can build specialized components that can handle your exact output format, then use them like any built-in Gradio component.

Detection Viewer: A custom viewer for object detection, instance segmentation, and pose estimation results. Renders bounding boxes, segmentation masks, keypoints, and skeleton connections — all in a reusable gr.HTML subclass that plugs directly into your model pipeline.

The community's built some creative components with gr.HTML too:

3D Camera Control for Image Editing: A full Three.js viewport inside a Gradio app! Drag handles to control azimuth, elevation, and distance. Your uploaded image appears in the 3D scene, and the camera parameters feed directly into Qwen's latest image editing model. These kinds of interactive 3D controls would normally require a separate frontend — with Gradio it's just one gr.HTML subclass🔥

Real-time Speech Transcription: Live transcription with Mistral's Voxtral model. The transcript display is a custom gr.HTML component with animated status badges, a live WPM counter, and styled output that updates as you speak. Real-time UI feedback without using React!

Every gr.HTML component takes three templates:

${value} injects Python state. props.value updates it from JavaScript. trigger('change') syncs back to Python. That's the whole API.

For reusable components, subclass gr.HTML:

Now Heatmap() works like gr.Image() or gr.Slider() — use it in Blocks, wire up event handlers, whatever you need.

When you ask your LLM to build a custom component, single-file output is everything. No "now create the styles file" or "wire this into your build config." Just one Python file that runs immediately.

The feedback loop becomes: describe what you want → get code → gradio app.py → see it working → describe what to fix → repeat. Each cycle takes seconds with Gradio's reload mode.

Deploy to Spaces with gradio deploy or share a temporary link with demo.launch(share=True). Within a few seconds from an idea to a live app.

Gradio ships with 32 interactive components, but sometimes your perfect AI web app needs something special. That's where gr.HTML comes in.

If you’ve got an idea, try building it with gr.HTML: describe what you want to your LLM, generate the code, run it. You might be surprised what you can ship in 5 minutes.

#10091. IBM and UC Berkeley Diagnose Why Enterprise Agents Fail Using IT-Bench and MAST

Ayhan Sebin Saurabh Jha Rohan Arora Daby Sow Mert Cemri Melissa Pan Ion Stoica

ITBench HF Space ITBench HF Dataset MAST HF Dataset ITBench Github MAST Github

IBM Research and UC Berkeley collaborated to study how agentic LLM systems break in real-world IT automation, for tasks involving incident triage, logs/metrics queries, and Kubernetes actions in long-horizon tool loops.

Benchmarks typically reduce performance to a single number, telling you whether an agent failed but never why. To solve this black-box problem, we applied MAST (Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy), an emerging practice for diagnosing agentic reliability ). By leveraging MAST to analyze ITBench—the industry benchmark for SRE, Security, and FinOps automation—we turned raw execution traces into structured failure signatures, revealing exactly what broke and how to fix it. We annotated 310 ITBench SRE traces across three distinct model classes: Gemini-3-Flash, Kimi-K2, and GPT-OSS-120B.

Takeaways from our analysis when building agents:

If you’re building agents for enterprise IT workflows, this is the kind of evaluation you want: not just “did it pass?”, but “what broke, where, and what intervention is most leverageable?”

Benchmarks like ITBench are becoming the standard for measuring agentic performance in high-stakes IT automation tasks. In ITBench, agents act as Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) or Security Analysts tasked with diagnosing Kubernetes outages, patching vulnerabilities, or managing cloud costs in production environments.

This benchmarks use success rate as a main metric to evaluate agents. However, this metric is insufficient for engineering robust systems. Knowing that an agentic system achieves a 14% success rate on ITBench tells us that it failed, but not why: Did it fail because it forgot the context? Because it hallucinated a command? Or because it simply did not terminate?

Without a comprehensive approach to diagnose these failures, developers are left guessing, often resorting to blind prompting tweaks that solve one problem only to create another.

As a new standard to analyze the failure modes of complex agentic systems, we developed MAST (Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy). MAST brings more insights and open up the opaque evaluation of these benchmarks. Derived from a rigorous analysis of over 1,600 traces across seven different frameworks, MAST provides a standardized taxonomy for agent failures.

MAST converts unstructured execution logs into structured "failure vectors" based on 14 distinct patterns across three key categories:

We stress-test the idea of using MAST to make agent evaluations actionable and gain insights on the failure modes by applying it to ITBench, a popular evaluation suite for IT automation tasks across SRE, Security/Compliance, and FinOps.

We annotated 310 ITBench SRE execution traces produced by an SRE agent built with Codex in realistic environments. These traces capture natural language interactions between agents and their tools across three models representing different capability tiers: Gemini-3-Flash, Kimi-K2, and GPT-OSS-120B. This lets us look past simple success metrics and investigate the distinct failure signatures driving these results. For this we use the recall scores, as the models by design only output a maximum of 3-5 outputs and SREs prefer the recall scores over F-1 score.

Below, we detail the findings from this diagnostic analysis.

When we examine the failed traces, a clear hierarchy of complexity becomes apparent across the three models. This is measured by the number of distinct failure modes observed per failed run.

This disparity in failure mode density reveals a fundamental difference in how these systems break down. Gemini-3-Flash exhibits a surgical failure profile. Even in unsuccessful runs, it maintains high internal coherence and typically fails due to a single isolated failure, such as an incorrect verification step. These failures are precise and far easier to diagnose.

On the opposite end of the spectrum, GPT-OSS-120B suffers from cascading collapse. In these traces, we observe that errors tend to compound over time. A small reasoning mismatch early in the process often leads to a deviation from the task specification, which in turn triggers a total derailment of the agent. Kimi-K2 represents the middle ground, where failures are more frequent and complex than the frontier model but do not reach the systemic instability seen in the 120B open weights model.

The significance of this finding is that a higher success rate is often accompanied by isolated failure. Systems that fail with fewer simultaneous problems are far more predictable and simpler to improve through targeted engineering interventions.

Perhaps the most critical insight from MAST is distinguishing between failures that the system can tolerate versus those that are fatal to success of the downstream task. By comparing the distribution of failure modes in Successful Traces vs. Failed Traces, we can classify them into three categories.

Across all three models, certain failure modes appear frequently even in runs that ultimately succeed. These are often structural frictions rather than terminal bugs.

This separation is where MAST proves its value. It allows us to ignore the bening failures like repetition that often occurs in troubleshooting, and focus instead on fatal failures that killed a run.

Certain behaviors strongly separate success from failure. When these modes appear, the probability of a successful outcome drops precipitously. The most prominent example is FM-3.3 (Incorrect Verification). This mode shows a 52 percent increase in failed Gemini-3-Flash traces compared to its successful ones. Other prominent failure modes are 1.5 (Unaware of Termination Conditions) and 2.6 (Reasoning Action Mismatch).

If these happen, the run is likely dead; guiding practitioners to develop robust context management strategies across agents in the system and multiple turns of interactions.

Gemini-3-Flash is highly efficient, but its primary bottleneck is its tendency to assume success without rigorous proof. Its failure signature is dominated by a massive delta in verification errors. It often identifies the correct signals but terminates before cross-referencing them against the ground truth. To fix this, developers should implement an external verification gate. By requiring tool-based evidence like a cleared alert or a healthy metric threshold before allowing the agent to exit, we can mitigate this model’s inherent overconfidence.

While termination confusion (FM-3.1 and FM-1.5) is the prevalent failure mode for Kimi-K2, its failed trajectories are defined by a pervasive Action-Reasoning Mismatch (FM-2.6), which is present in a staggering 92% of its failures.

Kimi-K2 is a good example of an overthinking model, its reasoning chains are often too long but can fail at execution.

GPT-OSS-120B exhibits the most unstable failure signature of the cohort. This model exhibits an average of 5.3 distinct failure modes per failed trace, indicating a fundamental inability to maintain internal state.

In summary, MAST lets you split failure modes into two buckets:

These are failures which are not fatal and from which the system can recover to successfully complete the task.

These are failures from which the system typically cannot recover.

This is the “richer understanding” piece: two models can have the same success rate on a small slice, yet fail for entirely different reasons—requiring different fixes.

MAST is a tool that inspects the agentic system traces to identify fine-grain failure types that support system development and debugging. In this blog, we show that by applying MAST to ITBench, we move from generic observations ("Open models struggle") to a concrete engineering roadmap that help improving the performance of agentic systems relying on thse models, e.g.:

#10089. The Hidden Problems Behind Website-to-CRM Integrations (and How to Prevent Them)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Connecting a website form to a customer relationship management (CRM) system may seem straightforward. A developer collects information from a form, sends it to an API endpoint, and checks whether a new contact appears in the CRM.

The integration may work perfectly during the first test. However, problems can appear after the website goes live. Some leads may not reach the CRM, duplicate contacts may appear, or important customer information may be missing.

These issues are not always easy to notice. A visitor might see a confirmation message even when the CRM has failed to save their information.

This guide explains common problems in website-to-CRM integrations and practical ways developers can prevent them.

A website-to-CRM integration allows information collected through a website to move into a CRM system. This usually happens through an API or webhook.

For example, when someone completes a contact form, the website collects their name, email address, phone number, and other details. The integration then sends this information to the CRM, where it can be stored and used by the relevant team.

An API integration provides a structured way for two applications to exchange information. Developers who need additional background can also read OpenHerald's overview of API integration.

The process usually involves several steps:

The website validates the submitted information.

The application sends a request to the CRM.

The CRM checks the request and processes the data.

The website or backend handles the response.

Each step needs to work correctly. If one part fails, the information may not reach its destination.

One important rule is to avoid displaying a successful submission message before the application has safely accepted and stored the data.

Data issues are among the most frequent problems in website-to-CRM integrations. They may not appear during development because test submissions usually contain simple, predictable information.

Real visitors enter data in different formats and may submit the same form more than once.

A visitor might complete a contact form and later download a resource using the same email address. If the integration creates a new CRM record every time, the same person may appear several times.

To prevent this, developers should decide how existing contacts will be identified.

Email addresses are commonly used for matching. Before comparing them, the application should remove unnecessary spaces and convert the address to a consistent format.

These values should be treated consistently.

Where supported, an upsert operation can create a new contact or update an existing one instead of creating unnecessary duplicates.

Website forms and CRM systems do not always use the same field structure.

A website may collect a visitor's full name in one field, while the CRM expects separate first-name and last-name values. Other fields may have different names or requirements.

Developers should create a clear mapping between website fields and CRM fields before building the integration.

They should also check which fields are required. If the CRM requires information that the website does not collect, the request may fail.

Different systems may store information in different formats.

For example, one application might use United Kingdom, while another expects UK. Dates, phone numbers, and country values can also create problems.

A reliable integration should validate and standardise these values before sending them to the CRM.

A contact record is more useful when the sales or marketing team knows where the visitor came from.

However, integrations sometimes send only basic contact information and leave out details such as campaign source, landing page, and referral information.

Developers should identify which tracking fields are useful and include them in the integration where appropriate.

Even an integration that works correctly at launch can stop working later.

Authentication credentials may expire, permissions may change, or an API provider may limit the number of requests an application can make.

Three areas deserve particular attention.

Many APIs use access tokens or other credentials to verify requests. Some tokens expire and must be refreshed.

If an application does not handle token renewal correctly, requests may begin failing without an obvious problem on the website.

Developers should implement the authentication process recommended by the CRM provider and monitor failed requests.

An API provider may restrict the number of requests allowed within a particular period.

A marketing campaign can suddenly increase website traffic and generate more form submissions than usual. If the integration exceeds the provider's limit, some requests may be rejected.

The application should recognise rate-limit responses and retry requests according to the provider's instructions.

An integration should not receive more access than it needs.

For example, a form submission service may only need permission to create or update contacts. Giving it full administrative access increases unnecessary security risks.

Use the minimum permissions required for the integration to function.

External services can experience outages, network delays, and temporary errors. If the website sends a form submission directly to the CRM without storing it first, a failed request could mean a lost lead.

A safer approach is to separate receiving a submission from delivering it to the CRM.

Validate the form information on the server.

Store the submission safely in your own system.

Send it to the CRM through a background process.

Retry temporary failures after an appropriate delay.

Flag permanent failures for manual review.

This approach gives the application another opportunity to deliver information when the CRM becomes available again.

A request might reach the CRM successfully, but the response could be lost because of a network problem. The website may then retry the same request, creating a duplicate contact.

Idempotency helps prevent this situation. The application can use a stable identifier for each submission so that repeating the same operation does not create another record.

For example, a combination of the form ID and a normalised email address may help identify repeated submissions. The exact approach depends on the CRM's API capabilities.

This is an illustrative example. Functions such as crmUpsertContact() and scheduleRetry() need to be implemented according to the application and CRM being used.

The important point is that every submission should have a known status: successfully delivered, waiting for another attempt, or requiring manual attention.

A working integration should also protect the quality and security of the information it collects.

Public forms can receive automated submissions from bots. Without appropriate protection, these entries can fill the CRM with unwanted records.

Validation should happen on the server, even if the website already checks information in the browser.

Some forms collect permission to send marketing communications.

If a visitor selects a consent checkbox, that information should also be passed to the CRM. Otherwise, the CRM may contain the contact details without a reliable record of the visitor's choice.

Where relevant, store the consent value, the wording or version displayed, and the time the visitor gave consent.

An integration should only send the information needed for its intended purpose.

Collecting unnecessary personal details increases the amount of information the application must protect and maintain.

Developers should also understand where submitted information is stored, including databases, queues, application logs, and the CRM.

Testing an integration before launch is important, but monitoring it afterwards is just as necessary.

A successful test does not prove that every future submission will work.

The following checks can help identify problems early.

Compare the number of website form submissions with the number of contacts successfully created or updated in the CRM.

A growing difference between the two numbers may indicate that some requests are failing.

Application logs should record the reason a request failed and include a submission identifier where possible.

Avoid storing complete personal details in logs unless there is a specific, justified need.

Developers should configure notifications when the integration's failure rate exceeds an acceptable threshold.

This makes it easier to investigate problems before they affect a large number of submissions.

A scheduled test submission can help confirm that the complete process is still working.

For example, a test lead can be sent periodically and checked to confirm that it reaches the CRM correctly.

Someone should be responsible for monitoring the integration.

This person or team should review errors, check API changes, monitor credentials, and investigate changes to CRM fields.

Without a clear owner, small problems can remain unnoticed for a long time.

Documentation makes integrations easier to maintain and troubleshoot.

It does not need to be complicated. A short reference document covering the main rules can save considerable time when another developer needs to work on the system.

Before deployment, developers should also test unusual situations.

Testing these situations helps reveal weaknesses that ordinary form submissions may not expose.

What is the most common website-to-CRM integration problem?

Duplicate contacts and incorrect field mapping are common problems. They usually happen when the website and CRM handle data differently.

How can developers prevent duplicate contacts?

Normalise email addresses, use a consistent matching rule, and use an upsert operation or idempotency mechanism where the CRM supports it.

Should a website send form data directly to a CRM?

For more reliable handling, the application should first validate and safely store the submission. A background process can then deliver it to the CRM and retry temporary failures.

How can I tell if a CRM integration has stopped working?

Compare website submission counts with CRM records, monitor failed requests, and schedule regular test submissions.

Who should be responsible for maintaining the integration?

Assign a developer or technical team to monitor the connection, review errors, maintain credentials, and respond to API changes.

Developers can make these integrations more reliable by validating information on the server, storing submissions before delivery, using safe retry mechanisms, and monitoring the results after launch.

The goal is simple: every valid submission should reach the CRM, and every failed submission should be visible and recoverable rather than silently lost.
